title: What’s new in OKF v0.3: enterprise-ready knowledge, use cases, and skills
raw_text:
In June we introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF) , an open specification that provides plain markdown and YAML to give agents the context they need. In July, v0.2 added trust signals: provenance, trust, freshness, lifecycle, and attestation. In production, bundles move between organizations, multiple agents edit the same corpus, and independent tools need to read a bundle the same way. Released today, OKF v0.3 adds precise conformance rules, trust tiers that keep pace with agent edits, self-describing bundles with licensing, safe ways to retire and move knowledge, a stable extension model, and a clear versioning policy. However, the core idea behind OKF stays the same: type is still the only required field, and your existing bundles keep working. We're also launching OKF use cases , which are community guides for using OKF alongside other industry standards, and two agent skills that let coding agents write and read OKF bundles. Finally, to make cross-organization collaboration easier, we’re moving OKF out of the Google Cloud Platform GitHub org into a standalone organization at https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/ . Let’s take a closer look at what’s new in OKF v0.3. Built for interoperability v0.3 adds a formal conformance section, allowing independent producers and consumers to work together by design. The spec is self-contained and uses RFC 2119 keywords. It gives one clear answer to the questions that come up when tools from different teams and vendors read the same bundle. The full detail is in the spec, but a few themes matter for anyone building on OKF: Built on standard file formats. OKF uses a small, widely supported set of standards: YAML 1.2 frontmatter, CommonMark with GFM tables and footnotes, and RFC 3339 timestamps. If your tools handle those, they handle OKF. OKF bundles share space with other markdown files. A .md file without a type is skipped by OKF consumers, so README.md , AGENTS.md , CONTRIBUTING.md , and SKILL.md can live inside a bundle without breaking it. Files that aren't markdown, like images or attester code, are assets that concepts can link to. Consumers handle real-world input predictably. Bundles written by many agents can contain nulls, empty strings, single values where a list was expected, and new vocabulary. v0.3 specifies how a consumer reads each of these. Consumers accept these inputs without failing, while validators log warnings for malformed entries. A bundle never fails because an optional field is missing or a link is broken. Trust that keeps pace with agents v0.2 gave every concept a trust tier: unverified , machine-confirmed , or human-reviewed . As agents take on more of the editing, v0.3 makes sure the tier always reflects the latest version of the content. Here's a typical sequence: A person reviews a metric definition and signs off. A week later, an agent refines the definition. The trust tier now reflects that the person hasn't yet reviewed the new text. In v0.3, only current verifications count . A verification is current when it happened at or after the last meaningful change to the content, recorded in generated.at : code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'generated: { by: reference_agent/gemini-2.5-pro, at: "2026-09-02T10:00:00Z" }
verified:
 - { by: "human:jsmith", at: "2026-08-25T09:00:00Z" } # before the rewrite: history
 - { by: "process:finance-nightly", at: "2026-09-03T02:00:00Z" } # current'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fa1681f2510>)])]> This concept is now machine-confirmed , not human-reviewed, until a person confirms it again. The older sign-off stays in the file as history, and a UI can show it as "reviewed before the last change." v0.3 also standardizes actor identifiers. Actors are <producer>/<version> for tools, or <scheme>:<id> for everything else, and v0.3 adds team: next to human: and process: . Only human: earns human-reviewed, because a team name doesn't say which person actually checked the content. Bundles that describe themselves When an agent has access to dozens of bundles, bundle-level metadata supports progressive disclosure so it can pick the right bundle without reading every file. In v0.3, the bundle-root index.md can carry frontmatter about the bundle itself: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '---
okf_version: "0.3"
title: Acme retail analytics
description: Tables, metrics, and sanctioned computations for Acme retail. Use it for sales and margin questions.
license: CC-BY-4.0
---'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fa14adbf050>)])]> description is written for routing. In one sentence it says what the bundle covers and when to use it. license makes clear what you're allowed to do with knowledge you receive from someone else. okf_version tells a consumer which rules to apply, including compatibility fallbacks for older bundles. Tools that regenerate index.md must keep this frontmatter. A lifecycle with forwarding addresses Knowledge evolves, and an agent that finds a deprecated concept should be able to get to its replacement. v0.3 adds superseded_by : code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'status: deprecated
superseded_by: /metrics/gross-margin.md'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fa14adbf590>)])]> Consumers that filter to current knowledge follow the pointer and return the replacement. The same mechanism handles moves and renames. Leave a short deprecated concept at the old path that points to the new one, and existing links and stored references keep working. One rule for links and paths Links in the body and path fields in frontmatter ( resource , superseded_by , executor.resource , and others) now resolve the same way: A value with a scheme ( https: ) is an absolute URL. A value that starts with / resolves from the bundle root. Anything else resolves from the directory of the file that contains it, just like on GitHub or in any markdown editor. For bundles marked v0.2 or earlier, or with no version, a consumer can also resolve paths from the bundle root, so existing bundles keep working. v0.3 also makes explicit that links are not parent/child relationships. Only the directory tree defines hierarchy. A link is an untyped, directed relationship, and the text around it says what kind ("joins with," "replaces," "depends on"). Path fields that point at concepts are edges in the bundle graph too. Room to extend, without collisions The community has been extending OKF since v0.1, with typed edges, routing hints, and erasure profiles. v0.3 makes a few extension mechanisms a first-class rule: Extension keys are allowed at any level , including inside sources entries, verified events, executor , and attester . A producer that edits a file must keep the keys it doesn't understand so one tool doesn't overwrite metadata added by another. Future OKF versions will never define keys that start with x- . Name your keys x-<producer>-<name> , for example x-acme-owner , and they won't collide with a future spec version. A versioning policy before 1.0 v0.3 defines OKF's versioning rules. Before 1.0, minor versions may include breaking changes as long as each is documented with a consumer fallback where possible. Starting at 1.0, minor versions will be strictly additive, and released normative text will not change in place. The spec also lists what was considered and deferred : typed relationships, the full attestation runtime protocol (receipt and verdict wire formats), semantic-layer attestation, validity windows, and a refuted verification event. Until the community agrees on a form for these, extension keys are the place to experiment. We'd like your proposals. Introducing OKF use cases OKF keeps its core specification small and links to existing domain schemas like Avro, Protobuf, or OpenAPI instead of duplicating them. In practice, though, when your organization already has an established artifact in another standard, such as a schema, a contract, or a spec, what should the OKF concept next to it say, and how should an agent use the two together? Starting with v0.3, we're publishing use cases : guides for using OKF with other industry standards. Each one explains: Where the boundary sits : what belongs in the other standard and what belongs in OKF. How to link the two : which frontmatter and link conventions point from a concept into the other artifact. What an agent should do with the combination. A complete worked example you can copy. Use cases are layered on the core spec, not part of it. A bundle that ignores them is still a conformant OKF bundle. When a convention proves itself across several use cases, it can be proposed for the core spec through the usual process. Use cases are managed directly in GitHub. Each use case gets its own folder under usecases/ in the OKF repository, for example usecases/<usecase>/ . The guide is a .md file in that folder, and any sample bundles or artifacts sit next to it. Use cases are reviewed, versioned, and discussed like any other change. Propose a use case If you pair OKF with a standard, please send us a proposal. A rough first draft is welcome. Open a pull request that adds a folder under usecases/ with a .md file in it, and we'll refine it together in review. Compatibility v0.3 has two breaking changes, and existing v0.2 bundles stay readable: Path fields resolve relative to their file. Fallback: for bundles marked v0.2 or earlier, or with no version, consumers can resolve from the bundle root. Only current verifications count toward the trust tier. No fallback needed, since tiers can only go down. Everything else is a clarification or an optional addition. v0.1 fallbacks ( timestamp , body # Citations ) still apply. Agent skills for OKF The two skills live in the new repository and follow the open Agent Skills format, so any agent that supports skills can load them. okf-generate writes, updates, migrates, and validates bundles from available sources. It cites a source for each claim, records a human review only when that person confirms it, and copies attested computations from a sanctioned source instead of writing them. okf-consume answers questions from a bundle. For each concept used, it reports the trust tier, status, freshness, and attestation result, and runs attested computations only through the bundle's configured executor and attester. To install them in Gemini CLI, run: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# install okf-generate
gemini skills install https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format --path skills/okf-generate

# install okf-generate
gemini skills install https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format --path skills/okf-consume'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fa14adbdb90>)])]> The README lists the install steps for other agents. Get involved Read the v0.3 spec . Add okf_version to your bundles, and check that your consumer computes trust tiers from current verifications only. Issues and pull requests, including new use case proposals, are welcome on GitHub. Spec, samples, use cases, and reference implementations: https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/
summary: In June we introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF) , an open specification that provides plain markdown and YAML to give agents the context they need. In July, v0.2 added trust signals: provenance, trust, freshness, lifecycle, and attestation. In production, bundles move between organizations, multiple agents edit the same corpus, and independent tools need to read a bundle the same way. Released today, OKF v0.3 adds precise conformance rules, trust tiers that keep pace with agent edits, self-describing bundles with licensing, safe ways to retire and move knowledge, a stable extension model, and a clear versioning policy.

title: Testing changes, fast: Introducing agentic assessments in Database Center
raw_text: Applying recommendations to a production database can feel risky if you can’t easily quantify the performance benefit or justify the additional cost. While Database Center flags fleet-level health issues and provides proactive recommendations, database administrators still face the challenge of testing recommended changes without disrupting live applications or spending hours manually configuring staging replicas. To help solve this problem, we’re excited to announce the preview of assessments in Database Center for Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL . Assessments is an agentic workflow that lets you run automated, isolated synthetic benchmarks on cloned instances, helping you verify potential performance gains before touching your production environment. Moving from recommendations to production changes Managing production databases means balancing system stability, performance, and infrastructure spend. When Database Center alerts you to a potential bottleneck and recommends a change, you need to evaluate the change before you can implement it. That workflow can be complex: Setting up dedicated staging environments to mirror production settings Running benchmark workloads to simulate real-world traffic Measuring latency, throughput, and resource saturation before and after applying changes Calculating whether performance gains justify potential cost adjustments Because this manual benchmarking process takes a lot of time and engineering effort, it’s easy to put off making critical updates, leaving databases under-provisioned or inefficient. How assessments automates the validation workflow Assessments simplify performance validation by automating the entire testing cycle in an isolated environment. When you click "Assess impact" on a supported recommendation in Database Center, the assessments workflow handles each step of the benchmarking process: Plan creation: Assessments builds a customized test plan for running a synthetic benchmark tailored to your instance. You can refine parameters such as client connections, transaction counts, query mode, or benchmark duration using plain-language prompts to match your target workload requirements (for example, "Change the benchmark duration to 60 seconds" ). Safe isolation: The agentic workflow clones your primary instance so that benchmarks run without consuming production resources or affecting live traffic. Baseline measurement: The workflow automatically runs synthetic workloads against the cloned instance to establish performance metrics from before the change. Applying changes: The workflow modifies the cloned environment according to the selected recommendation. Comparative reporting: Finally, it reruns the benchmark workload and generates an evaluation report comparing pre- and post-change metrics, including transaction throughput, average latency, CPU utilization, and memory usage — and automatically deletes the temporary clone once the assessment completes. Initial supported recommendations During the preview, you can run automated assessments for three types of Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL updates: Machine upgrade: Measure how increased vCPU and memory allocations impact query throughput and reduce compute contention under load. Edition upgrade: Compare performance metrics between Cloud SQL Enterprise and Enterprise Plus editions to verify throughput gains and reduced latency. Enable data cache: Evaluate how enabling data cache on Enterprise Plus instances affects read latency and offloads I/O bottlenecks for data-intensive workloads. Get started Assessments in Database Center are available in preview. You can start validating performance changes in your Cloud SQL for Postgres environment today directly in the Google Cloud console: Review the release notes for the latest updates on Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. Read the assessments overview to explore architecture details and supported database versions. Follow the step-by-step guide to create an assessment for your instances in Database Center.

To help solve this problem, we’re excited to announce the preview of assessments in Database Center for Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL . Assessments is an agentic workflow that lets you run automated, isolated synthetic benchmarks on cloned instances, helping you verify potential performance gains before touching your production environment.

title: Sashiko: Lessons from building an agentic code review system for Linux
raw_text:
The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers. Some of those patches are solid changes, just written faster; many others are plausible-looking "AI slop" sent by contributors who do not fully understand the systems they are modifying. And the influx of AI-generated security reports, many of which are duplicates or inaccurate, only adds to maintainers’ load. Linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer. It spans more than 35 million lines of code, and over 85,000 changes land every year. Automated build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch build errors and crashes, but code review has always been the main way to guarantee the stability and safety of the kernel. Every day, maintainers read hundreds and hundreds of proposed patches by hand to catch memory leaks, deadlocks, race conditions, and security bugs. To help maintainers handle the load and catch bugs before they land, the Google AI & Infrastructure team built Sashiko , an open-source, agentic code review system powered by Gemini. We named the project after the Japanese word 刺し子, a stitching technique for artistically reinforcing worn cloth, and donated it to the Linux Foundation earlier this year. In this blog, we cover the problem Sashiko was designed to solve, how it works, what the data shows, and what we learned from building and running it in the wild. Reviewing code is hard Reviewing a change in a complex code base is objectively hard, both for humans and LLMs. It often requires a deep understanding of how the system works in general, well outside the proposed change. In fact, it’s pretty common to see patches that engineers claim perfectly solve the problem, but if they were to be merged, would actually introduce even worse problems (albeit subtle). Traditionally, only experienced maintainers have been able to spot and prevent these issues. The same is true for agentically generated code. To verify the correctness of a change, a potentially large number of invariants should be proven, which is often a much larger and harder task than developing the change itself. This is true for both human and agentic reviewers. However, LLM-based reviewers have some unique properties, both positive and negative: LLMs often struggle to put in enough effort. LLMs are trained to achieve the goal of spending fewer tokens. So they often tend to cut corners and dismiss concerns without proper investigation or flag false positives without proper due diligence. LLMs are easier to bias . The current generation of LLMs usually performs much better if provided a single relatively simple task (e.g., prove the patch for memory leaks) rather than multiple tasks (e.g., explore several complex, varied concerns). It’s pretty common for an LLM to find an obvious issue in the code and refuse to look deeper for other types of issues. Also, commit log text can sometimes affect the result of code review in a non-predicatable or even malicious way. LLMs don’t have persistent memory. Surprisingly, this is a positive thing for code review: An LLM can review the same or similar patch multiple times as if it were a new patch. No sane human can review the same patch applied to 100 slightly different branches to find the few that have incompatible changes. How Sashiko reviews a patch To avoid these failure modes, Sashiko separates finding candidate bugs from verification of those bugs , and requires each pass to record what it ruled out: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Gather context and plan
 -> Parallel specialist sessions (concerns + dismissed concerns)
 -> Triage
 -> Per-bug deep checks
 -> Review report'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fa14bf07e50>)])]> Notes on each step: Gather context and plan: Sashiko first pulls in the code around the diff (modified functions, struct definitions, and direct callers) and loads the subsystem's domain guides, so the changed lines are never judged in isolation. A planner then decides which specialist passes are needed (skipping hardware checks on pure software code, for example) and sets a reasoning budget for each pass based on patch complexity. Parallel specialist sessions: Up to seven specialist sessions run in parallel, each focused on a single class of problems: commit intent, implementation match, control flow, resource lifetimes, locking, security, and hardware. Giving each pass a single focus prevents one type of bug from crowding out another. Each session searches and reads the repository with git tools (averaging about 100 tool calls per review) and outputs two lists: concerns it believes are real, and candidate concerns it investigated and ruled out, along with the code that supports that conclusion. Triage: A lead verifier audits those two lists together. Clear-cut bugs already proven by the code in front of it pass straight through; dismissals proven by a local check are dropped. Everything else deserves additional investigation. Crucially, that includes not only contested bugs where specialists disagreed, but also shaky self-dismissals — cases where a specialist spotted a real bug and dismissed it by assuming, without proof, that some unseen caller or lock would prevent it. Per-bug deep checks: Instead of checking all difficult cases in one shared prompt, Sashiko gives each difficult case its own verification agent that runs in parallel. Each agent gets one specific question to answer with git tools under a symmetrical rule: Neither a bug claim nor a dismissal is accepted without concrete code proof across all call sites. If a specialist talks itself out of a real bug based on a false assumption, this step catches it and promotes it back to a real finding. Review report: Sashiko generates a report that sounds like a human maintainer asking questions about the proposed change, matching the style expected on a Linux mailing list. All this happens at no cost for developers. Deep agentic reviews at scale require a substantial token budget. If developers had to pay for them with their own API keys, many important contributors would be pushed away. Instead, Sashiko reviews patches sent to public Linux kernel mailing lists, and Google runs the service at sashiko.dev . Everything runs in the open: every prompt, tool call, reasoning step, and ruled-out bug is public. The project initially used the open-source Linux review prompts started by Chris Mason, and more than 100 contributors, including prominent kernel maintainers and engineers, have since helped to improve prompts and Sashiko itself. Recently, Sashiko switched to a different prompt system that combines per-tree or per-version auto-generated notes on code with subjective maintainers notes, which contain directions and instructions from maintainers that can’t be derived from the code. What the data shows The real test of an automated reviewer is whether maintainers pay attention to the reports it sends out, and whether those reports track actual software quality. Seven months of Sashiko production data from the kernel mailing lists give a clear picture of both these questions. It is part of the daily workflow. Sashiko completes roughly 1200 reviews a day across over 100 kernel mailing lists. It sends review emails only to lists whose maintainers opt in, and already over 70 of them have done so. Developers also engage directly with the reports: More than 1500 kernel developers have replied on the mailing lists, and their pushback on false alarms has directly driven improvements to Sashiko's prompts and verification engine. In fact, LWN.net recently wrote that Sashiko has already become an important part of the kernel's development process and was the top bug reporter of issues in the 7.2 release cycle. It prevents new bugs and uncovers old ones. When Sashiko flags a bug in a proposed patch, the author typically fixes it in the next revision before the change is ever merged. Many developers run Sashiko locally or in corporate private instances. The bugs that Sashiko helped to prevent leave no trace in the git commit log, making them hard to count directly. What can be counted are fixes for preexisting bugs that Sashiko finds and reports as a byproduct of reviewing new changes: Sashiko is cited in over 2000 mainline kernel commits and in over 500 of this year's official Linux kernel CVEs, spanning drivers, core kernel code, networking, GPUs, memory management, and virtualization. Fewer bugs are slipping into mainline releases. Across the 18 kernel releases prior to Sashiko (Linux 6.2 through 6.19, covering 254000 commits), an average of 3.4% of merged commits required a follow-up fix within 60 days. Since Sashiko rolled out, that 60-day fix rate has fallen to 2.8% in Linux 7.1 and 2.2% in Linux 7.2, a 35% drop (with the 30-day fix rate falling from 2.3% to 1.4%). It’s too early to make strong claims, and obviously many other factors can influence release-to-release numbers, so we cannot solely credit Sashiko for the entire drop, but the trend is optimistic. Since Sashiko was rolled out, the percentage of merged commits in the Linux kernel that received a follow-up fix in 60 days has dropped by 35%. A clean review carries real signal. If Sashiko's warnings were mostly noise, commits merged with warnings would need follow-up fixes no more often than commits that passed cleanly. In practice, across 21,500 tracked mainline commits, patches that received a clean Sashiko review required a follow-up fix within 60 days just 0.9% of the time — less than a third of the historical baseline. Patches merged despite a critical Sashiko warning needed a fix 7.6% of the time — an 8x higher risk (and 6.3x higher even after adjusting for patch size). That gap is what makes Sashiko useful to maintainers: A clean pass instills real confidence, while a critical warning is a strong reason to take another look at the proposed patch. This all tracks with what Linus Torvalds wrote in a mailing-list discussion a few weeks after Sashiko’s launch: "As you say, Sashiko tends to be quite good. Even when it flags something unnecessarily and there's no actual problem, there's likely to be a reason for the question. And we've seen some truly stellar reports too. Things that are deep and subtle, and the AI is 100% correct. So anybody who thinks that all AI is slop is in denial about the current state." - Linus Torvalds ( on lore.kernel.org ) Sashiko at a glance Since March 2026 Patch reviews completed 241,000 (~1200+ / day) Opted-in kernel subsystem lists 75+ Mainline commits crediting Sashiko 2,000+ 2026 Linux kernel CVEs crediting Sashiko 528 60-day post-merge fix rate Down from 3.4% baseline to 2.2% (Linux 7.2) What we learned from building and running Sashiko First, benchmark-driven development beats intuition. While developing Sashiko, we tried many ideas that looked very reasonable on their face but didn’t end up working out. Other ideas were less obvious but worked surprisingly well. What was crucial: Early on, we built a benchmark out of nearly 1,000 real Linux kernel bugs and used it to evaluate every major Sashiko change. Every bug in this set was a real mistake that had passed human review by kernel experts, had been merged into mainline Linux, and later had to be fixed. On that benchmark, Sashiko with the new Gemini 4 Carbon model catches 75.8% of the bugs that human reviewers missed (using high thinking level). Second, coding agents are not great at reviewing their own code. Models are trained to produce a working solution within a limited token budget. Asking these agents to review their own code might work well for isolated tasks, but for real, large codebases, creating a functional solution is often just 5-10% of the work. What’s really hard is to produce a solution that works all of the time, is well-integrated into the surrounding code, and doesn’t introduce subtle regressions. This is often substantially more complex and requires additional effort. Similar to human developers, agents benefit from external code review: Reviewers often spot issues that the initial author missed, even if they are not more experienced. Third, open source and shared community ownership and development help to build trust. By being fully open and transparent from the beginning , Sashiko allowed anyone to run it the way they wanted: using different models (including open source and local models), customizing prompts, or even adopting Sashiko to other-than-Linux projects. This helped with community adoption and brought over 100 contributors to improve Sashiko, including some prominent kernel developers. More and more engineers are putting local Sashiko instances into their coding-agent loops, so patches are checked against the community's review rules before a human maintainer ever sees them. We use the same workflow to build Sashiko itself ("Sashiko for Sashiko"), running it to review every change to its codebase and prompt pipeline both locally and through a Github integration. Although Sashiko started in the Linux kernel, the need for an agentic trust layer applies across critical open-source software. Because the core review engine does not depend on C or on kernel-specific rules, the Linux kernel playbook (combining an open verification pipeline, community-owned domain guides, and a benchmark mined from historically known issues and fixes) can likely be applied to other foundational open-source projects such as GCC, LLVM, or Git. "Now, I think the other side of AI - and this is where Sashiko comes in - is that it basically does end up being a tool that can then increase the trust in the patch. So AI giveth, and AI taketh away. But the basic issue shouldn't be AI per se, it should be that notion of 'trust'." - Linus Torvalds on LKML You can check out Sashiko at sashiko.dev , or find the code on GitHub to run it in your own development workflow.
summary: The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers.

title: Building an agentic stack in Envoy: routing models, tokens, and MCP
raw_text: At Google Cloud, we believe the next generation of AI and agentic systems must be built on open, battle-tested foundations. Envoy, an open-source edge and service proxy designed for cloud-native applications, has already transformed microservices and modern cloud networking, powering everything from Google Cloud’s Application Load Balancers to the Agent Substrate dataplane on Google Kubernetes Engine. Now, Envoy is uniquely positioned to become the open standard for AI traffic, MCP tooling, and agent-to-agent communication. Earlier this year, we presented the technical case for Envoy networking in the agentic AI era , examining how autonomous AI agents fundamentally challenge traditional Layer 7 networking assumptions. Unlike microservices, autonomous agent workloads choose who they communicate with. In addition, their routing attributes live deep within request bodies, with their traffic governed by token budgets as well as request rates, and their multi-turn reasoning loops requiring stateful session affinity and strict tool execution boundaries. At Google Cloud, we have been working hard to develop Envoy for the agentic era. Read on for a closer look at how Envoy has evolved to better support autonomous agents, giving developers the performance and portability of an open-source ecosystem, backed by enterprise security and scalability. Why autonomous agents challenge traditional L7 proxies Over the past decade, Envoy became the industry standard for cloud-native traffic management by operating cleanly at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP connection management) and Layer 7 (URI, method, and header-based routing). Autonomous agents introduce two higher-order protocol layers: Layer 8 (agentic interaction protocols): such as LLM APIs , Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Google’s Agent2Agent (A2A) , running over JSON-RPC 2.0 or gRPC. Critical policy attributes—such as tools/call , tool_name: "execute_sql" , or model: "gemini-1.5-pro" —are serialized inside the request payload. Layer 9 (agent framework interfaces): Coordination frameworks such as UCP, AP2, and Google Cloud’s Agent Development Kit, where multi-turn workflows produce dynamic token consumption and non-linear execution graphs. Fronting these workloads with traditional L7 proxies creates four major architectural challenges: Payload blindness: Nearly all LLM traffic shares the same paths (such as /v1/chat/completions ), so a header-based proxy cannot distinguish between a low-cost query and an expensive 500,000-token prompt, or one model from another. Request rate limiting fallacy: One request per minute with a massive context window can use more accelerator compute and memory bandwidth than dozens of short queries, and agent loops can burn through budgets unnoticed. Stateless load balancing: Each turn of an agent's conversation should go back to the server that already remembers it. Traditional load balancers send it to whichever server is next, so the model has to start over for every turn, this wastes time and GPUs. Ungoverned tool execution: Agents query databases, execute code in sandboxes, and call third-party APIs. Without inline inspection of MCP tool calls, organizations risk prompt injection, data exfiltration, and runaway billing loops. The core pillars of Envoy’s agentic stack To address these challenges, Envoy provides capabilities that turn the network into an active governance layer: Core Pillar Operational Functionality 1. Native body parser Payload blindness: Read request bodies, not just headers. Line-rate payload normalization across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini schemas with SSE stream handling. 2. Tokenomics engine Request-rate fallacy: Count tokens, not just requests. Pre-inference token estimation, tokens per minute (TPM) / tokens per day (TPD) rate limiting 3. Model & MCP routing Stateless load balancing: Keep agent sessions on the right servers Endpoint Picker (EPP) model dispatch, KV-cache prefix affinity, MCP Stateless support. 4. AI security guardrails Ungoverned tool execution: Policy tool calls. Inline policy, decision point (ext_proc) callouts for guardrails: Model Armor, ShieldGemma, and data loss prevention. 1. Native wire-format body parsing and transcoding Client applications often get locked into specific model APIs. For example, client code built for OpenAI's schema cannot communicate with Anthropic's endpoints or Google’s Gemini without client-side translation layers. To help, Envoy ecosystem includes native body parsers that normalize requests across diverse model families, providing: Client abstraction: Upstream applications send a standardized schema. Envoy inspects the JSON payload at line-rate, extracts the target model, and dynamically transcodes the request into the downstream provider's native format. No application code changes: Switching from an external commercial model to a self-hosted open-source model (such as Gemma or Llama on vLLM) requires only an Envoy configuration update. Application code remains unchanged. Streaming token extraction: Envoy parses server-sent events (SSE) response streams in real time, capturing token counts from usage chunks while maintaining ultra-low time-to-first-token latency. 2. Tokenomics engine: token-aware traffic management In AI networking, tokens are the fundamental unit of capacity . Envoy replaces coarse request counters with token-aware traffic management features such as: Token rate limiting: Enforces tokens per minute (TPM) and tokens per day (TPD) limits per tenant, project, or model. Pre-inference throttling: Envoy estimates input tokens from request payload bytes and extracts actual token usage from LLM responses to record in a quota database, rejecting subsequent over-quota requests with an HTTP 429 before they reach the inference cluster. Runaway loop protection: Autonomous agents can enter recursive reasoning loops. By tracking cumulative token consumption and message counts per session or agent ID, Envoy throttles multi-turn sessions once an agent exceeds its assigned budget. 3. Model routing and Model Context Protocol (MCP) support Envoy manages traffic for both downstream model backends and outbound tool calls, with: KV-cache prefix affinity: Using the Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extensions and Endpoint Picker (EPP), Envoy routes prompts sharing identical system instructions to the GPU worker currently holding that cache in memory, reducing latency. Model retry and fallback: If a primary model returns a 429 status code or fails, Envoy automatically retries or redirects the request to a secondary model pool with zero client interruption. MCP tool routing: For MCP agents, Envoy routes requests via JSON-RPC 2.0 bodies and HTTP headers. Per the 2026-07-28 MCP specification , Envoy uses Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers for zero-body-parsing routing to backend servers. Backends reject header-body mismatches with an HTTP 400 / -32020 (HeaderMismatch) error to prevent tampering. 4. AI security guardrails Inline safety filtering cannot come at the expense of network throughput. To prevent this, Envoy provides security callouts: Using standardized external processing ( ext_proc ), Envoy connects to dedicated policy decision engines — such as Google Cloud’s Model Armor, ShieldGemma, or local classifiers — to detect prompt injections and sensitive data leaks with minimal latency overhead. High-density infrastructure: Envoy and Agent Substrate In enterprise production environments, agents frequently spend time idle between user queries or long-running tool executions. Running hundreds of thousands of idle agents in dedicated containers or virtual machines can create prohibitive infrastructure costs. Envoy pairs directly with high-density execution runtimes like Agent Substrate to provide: Scale-to-zero traffic steering: Agent Substrate uses lightweight isolation runtimes (such as Cloud Hypervisor, microVMs and gVisor application sandboxes) that can suspend and resume in milliseconds. When traffic arrives for a suspended agent, Envoy buffers the initial packet while signaling the runtime to resume the instance, completing the end-to-end resume in milliseconds. Egress perimeter defense: Envoy functions as both an ingress and egress gateway for agent environments, routing the inbound traffic and restricting outbound network calls to verified domains and preventing untrusted autonomous code from reaching unauthorized endpoints. Getting started Envoy has evolved into an intelligent, extensible networking layer designed specifically for the unique demands of multi-agent architectures. To begin building with the agentic stack in Envoy: Explore the code: Review the Envoy proxy and Agent Router implementations on Github and examine the open-source sample configurations. Join the community: Participate in CNCF, Gateway API , and Kubernetes AI Gateway Working Group to collaborate on standardized inference APIs, MCP routing specifications, and token management conventions.
summary: At Google Cloud, we believe the next generation of AI and agentic systems must be built on open, battle-tested foundations. Envoy, an open-source edge and service proxy designed for cloud-native applications, has already transformed microservices and modern cloud networking, powering everything from Google Cloud’s Application Load Balancers to the Agent Substrate dataplane on Google Kubernetes Engine. Now, Envoy is uniquely positioned to become the open standard for AI traffic, MCP tooling, and agent-to-agent communication. Earlier this year, we presented the technical case for Envoy networking in the agentic AI era , examining how autonomous AI agents fundamentally challenge traditional Layer 7 networking assumptions.

title: Scaling massive AI/ML workloads with IPv6 on Google Kubernetes Engine clusters
raw_text:
TL;DR: Single-stack IPv6 on GKE runs both nodes and pods without having to use private IPv4 addresses. Available in preview for Cloud TPU v6e and CPU node pools, including Axion, it works with DNS64/NAT64 to reach IPv4 endpoints. Long before they run out of compute or power, AI applications hit another wall: running out of IP addresses. A single AI deployment often requires a vast address space to support everything from thousands of accelerator nodes, scaling inference replicas, bursting Ray workers and pipelines, pod sidecars, and services like vector databases. Running a dual stack — IPv6 behind a private IPv4 space — can help, but only to a point, because the private IPv4 space has often already been exhausted across existing networks. To help, today, we're announcing single-stack IPv6 on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), allowing you to run both nodes and pods on IPv6, without private IPv4 addresses. Single-stack IPv6 is available in preview for Cloud TPU v6e and CPU node pools, including Axion, and works with DNS64/NAT64 to reach IPv4 endpoints. Nodes and pods run IPv6-only across Cloud TPU v6e and CPU-based node pools, with no private IPv4. Workloads reach Google Cloud APIs over native IPv6 and IPv4-only endpoints through DNS64/NAT64. What single-stack IPv6 delivers The availability of single-stack IPv6 in GKE is a game-changer for large AI deployments. Consider the following features and benefits that it brings to the table: 1. No private IPv4 required for nodes or pods Nodes and pods use IPv6 exclusively. Without the RFC 1918 footprint that governs private IPv4 address spaces, clusters avoid conflicts with on-premises networks, peered VPCs, or adjacent clusters. 2. IPv4 interoperability with DNS64/NAT64 You enable DNS64 on the VPC, and NAT64 on a regional Cloud NAT gateway, allowing pods to transparently reach IPv4-only endpoints, registries, and dataset hubs — refer to the documentation to learn how to configure DNS64 and set up Cloud NAT . 3. Massive address space per node Each node receives a /112 pod range (65,536 addresses), so IP address capacity no longer limits how high your clusters, nodes, or pods can scale. Standard GKE maximum-pods-per-node limits still apply. 4. Broad accelerator and compute support We designed single-stack IPv6 in GKE with the goal of supporting a range of accelerators and general compute families. At preview, it supports Cloud TPU v6e (Trillium), plus E2, N1, N2, N2D, N4, C3, C3D, C4, C4D, C4A, and Z3 machine families, with support for additional accelerators and machine families coming soon. 5. Direct workload observability Every pod has a unique IPv6 address without having to run NAT inside the cluster, simplifying telemetry, network policies, and debugging. Performance and scale Single-stack IPv6 removes private IPv4 address limits without additional data plane overhead. In our internal testing, we saw the following performance characteristics: Pod lifecycle: Burst pod scheduling and CNI sandbox setup performed at parity with IPv4. Networking : Inter-node TCP/UDP latency and multi-stream pod-to-pod throughput matched IPv4. Services and DNS : eBPF service load balancing and NodeLocalDNS showed no measurable overhead compared to standard IPv4. Start building today Single-stack IPv6 is available now in preview on GKE version 1.37.1-gke.3020000 To create your first IPv6-only cluster, run the following commands, replacing REGION and CLUSTER_NAME: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# 1. Create a VPC with internal (ULA) IPv6 enabled
gcloud compute networks create gke-ipv6-net \
 --subnet-mode=custom \
 --enable-ula-internal-ipv6

# 2. Enable DNS64 for the VPC
gcloud dns policies create gke-ipv6-dns64 \
 --networks=gke-ipv6-net \
 --enable-dns64-all-queries

# 3. Enable NAT64 in your region
gcloud compute routers create gke-ipv6-router \
 --network=gke-ipv6-net --region=REGION
gcloud compute routers nats create gke-ipv6-nat64 \
 --router=gke-ipv6-router --region=REGION \
 --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips \
 --nat64-all-v6-subnet-ip-ranges

# 4. Create the cluster
gcloud beta container clusters create CLUSTER_NAME \
 --cluster-version=1.37.1-gke.3020000 \
 --location=REGION \
 --enable-dataplane-v2 \
 --cluster-dns=clouddns \
 --stack-type=ipv6 \
 --network=gke-ipv6-net \
 --create-subnetwork name=my-subnet \
 --ipv6-access-type=internal'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fa14a8a4250>)])]> To learn more, see the documentation .

title: Do AI’s mathematical advances put PKI under threat?
raw_text: Warnings by a leading cryptographer that industry-wide public-key cryptography could fail because of advances in AI has sparked a debate in the security community. In a series of post on X, Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green warned that existing public-key cryptography systems were at risk because machines have begun outperforming humans in their ability to address some mathematical problems. “I think there is a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt, and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in our existing public-key encryption algorithms,” Green wrote last month. Green’s initial warning and follow-up comments offered a warning about the cryptographic foundations beneath public key infrastructure (PKI) , rather than an obituary for PKI, the system of certificates, keys, and certificate authorities that secures Transport Layer Security (TLS), code signing, and many other information security functions. “I’m worried about standardized public-key encryption (and some signatures) and specifically the fact that most of it is based on a small number of hard problems,” Green added . These hard mathematical problems have been extensively analyzed by humans for years but any comforting notion that this means they are safe is now being undermined because machines have begun outperforming humans in solving some mathematical problems. Green warns that a disruptive loss of confidence in internet security systems would arise if a major cryptanalytic surprise arrives faster than standards and deployments can adapt — so the industry needs to focus on improved cryptographic agility. The comments sparked a discussions on LinkedIn and elsewhere about how public-key crypto could fail . Green is yet to respond to CSO’s request for comment on the debate he sparked. Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, a cryptographer and professor at Finland’s Tampere University who has looked closely at AI-powered crypto-analysis , told CSO that he takes Green’s warning seriously but urges caution, saying there is no need to rip and replace established industry cryptographic standards. “We really can’t entirely rule out surprises, but I’d also definitely not recommend some hasty moves, because those are sure to cause problems,” Saarinen said. “Cryptography has good standards, best practices, and active modernization paths (the ‘PQC transition’) — just following those is the most sensible approach from information security perspective.” The math at stake Saarinen explained that there are two kinds of “hard problems” in mathematics: Numerical problems for which a solution is thought to be hard to compute (for computers) Analytic problems that are open and have been expected to be settled by a human with pencil and paper via a proof, counterexample, new theory, etc. “What has happened in 2026 is that mathematics had its ‘Lee Sedol moment’ (after the ‘last Go grandmaster’) and [analytical] problems previously thought to be in the human domain (2) are now being solved by computers,” Saarinen told CSO. Cryptography uses numerical problems in class — traditional ones like factoring the products of large prime numbers and discrete logarithm, and newer ones like learning with errors (LWE). Analyzing those algorithms and their complexity is part of theoretical computer science. “The fear in cryptography is that AI will find a shortcut for some hard computational problems and make them easy,” Saarinen said. “While AI is very good at optimizing computation, we don’t expect it to turn all hard computational problems into trivial ones.” 2026: Breaking HAWK and McEliece Cryptographic problems involving set (1) above are typically “sub-exponential”; solving them requires an almost exponential number of operations relative to the problem size or distance. “A cryptographically relevant break can be exponential but might halve the number of bits; such an analytic break has happened to some relatively new schemes, such as HAWK by AI in 2026 , and to numerous older proposals by humans,” Saarinen explained. AI also played a significant role in finding a significant shortcut to the parameters of the McEliece cryptosystem (one of the earliest public-key schemes, designed in 1978). “The German cyber agency had been recommending a variant called ‘Classic McEliece’ for quantum security since 2020, but withdrew its recommendation at the end of September,” Saarinen added. Saarinen clarified that, in both cases, the schemes could still be “considered secure if security parameters were adjusted, but that would have doubled public and secret keys, signatures, and ciphertexts.” Meanwhile, SA and Elliptic-Curve cryptosystems are already “broken” from a computational-complexity viewpoint because “polynomial-time quantum algorithms for them have been known since 1994, and building quantum computers is ‘just an engineering problem,’” according to Saarinen. The main post-quantum alternatives, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA, have received more than a decade of intense analysis. Looking for a ‘mathematical shortcut’ Another question that cryptographers are asking is whether public-key cryptography or symmetric cryptography is more vulnerable to AI cryptanalysis. Saarinen suggested a “mathematical shortcut” is more likely to exist in public-key cryptography given that it, by definition, requires mathematical structure for the “trapdoor” (a secret key that opens a public-key encrypted message or creates a signature that the public key can verify). “Symmetric-key cryptography (hashes and keyed ciphers) has simply more design freedom in this sense,” Saarinen concluded. Q-Day and LLMs Professor Alan Woodward, a computer scientist at the University of Surrey, said that LLMs are yet to make a huge dent on cryptography. “We’ve seen some inroads and erosion of the security guarantees, but what’s actually happening as far as I can see is that the LLMs are acting as a great tool for mathematicians, cryptographers, and computer scientists to speed up their research: that leap of intuition needed to find the fatal flaw still seems to need humans,” Prof. Woodward said. “LLMs are very effective at finding flaws in those implementations rather than the underlying mathematics.” Prof. Woodward compared the threat posed by AI in breaking encryption schemes to the danger to legacy encryption schemes posed by quantum computers. Both problems highlight the need for improved agility in the cryptographic schemes in use. “We’ve already seen people migrating in preparation for ‘Q-Day’ so in some ways that should already be addressing the risks posed, if they’re real, by LLMs,” according to Prof. Woodward, referring to the hypothetical future time when quantum computers are powerful enough to break public-key encryption. “The most effective route so far seems to be a hybrid route where we have a mix of cryptographic schemes that, whilst one or two might fall away, leaves us with others we can rely upon. Any found to be flawed for whatever reason can be deprecated rapidly and the intact schemes used instead.”
summary: Warnings by a leading cryptographer that industry-wide public-key cryptography could fail because of advances in AI has sparked a debate in the security community. In a series of post on X, Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green warned that existing public-key cryptography systems were at risk because machines have begun outperforming humans in their ability to address some mathematical problems. “I think there is a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt, and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in our existing public-key encryption algorithms,” Green wrote last month. Green’s initial warning and follow-up comments offered a warning about the cryptographic foundations beneath public key infrastructure (PKI) , rather than an obituary for PKI, the system of certificates, keys, and certificate authorities that secures Transport Layer Security (TLS), code signing, and many other information security functions.

title: A single pull request could have handed attackers the keys to Microsoft’s software supply chain
raw_text: The most dangerous actor in a software supply chain may now be an automated script with powerful credentials and no idea where it’s sending them. Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet), which sits on billions of devices worldwide. A single pull request could have tricked Microsoft’s internal tooling into freely handing over a moderator’s GitHub access token, with no phishing, no malware, no moderator clicking or approval required. There is currently no evidence that the flaw has been exploited in the wild. But it serves as a cautionary tale for enterprises that the automation they trust is becoming an attacker entry point, and package repositories are particularly enticing targets. “Package registries have become the highest-profile target in the software supply chain,” Moriel Harush , Cycode security research lead, wrote in a blog post . “Compromise a single maintainer, and you reach everyone who trusts them. Compromise the gatekeepers, and you reach the entire ecosystem.” Whatever the employee can do, the attacker can do WinGet is Microsoft’s free, open source command line tool that helps users discover, install, upgrade, configure, and remove apps. It exists on more than 1.4 billion active devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server 2025. WinGet’s catalog is a public GitHub repository , and its gatekeeper, so to speak, is a small, official group of Microsoft moderators who review a constant stream of community pull requests and proposed changes. By default, WinGet installations on every Windows machine trust the actions those keepers take. The hole is in the moderators’ own internal triage tool. This PowerShell helper attached the moderator’s secret GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) to any HTTP request, without checking who owned that address. This meant an attacker merely had to supply an address. Theoretically, if they opened a pull request and pointed an InstallerURL software installation package at their own server, “the trap was set,” Harush explained. Microsoft’s automated Azure DevOps validation pipeline would then attempt to fetch the URL, but the attacker’s server would intentionally return an error. This added a validation error label to the pull request. The moderator’s internal script would respond to that label by running a CheckInstaller routine which would send a HEAD request to the attacker via an authenticated HTTP helper, whose job is to automatically attach credentials or tokens to outgoing HTTP requests and handle authorization errors . Then all the attacker had to do was check their logs and extract the moderator’s official GitHub token, which was “casually” handed over. But the token is not merely a repository-scoped credential, it is a full identity credential, meaning whatever that Microsoft employee can do on GitHub, the token can do. Harush explained: “It is like a courier stapling your house key to every parcel that has your name on it, because most of them are destined for your own address.” But if a stranger uses your name and changes the address to one they control, “your key is delivered directly to them.” Armed with this key to Microsoft’s internal environment, an attacker could push malicious manifests, approve their own pull requests, and slip in backdoored installers to 14,000 exposed packages, all under a highly trusted, official Microsoft badge. They could also access and write to every other Microsoft repository the moderator had access to, modify GitHub Actions workflows across those repositories to achieve remote code execution (RCE) and exfiltrate corporate secrets. There is a precondition for this attack: At least one moderator has to have the triage tracker running in a continuous background loop, which it is designed to do as it waits for work. Underlying model ‘fundamentally flawed’ Harush pointed out that Microsoft’s C# version of the tool, in the same directory, did not share the flaw; as such, it would have offered safer authentication. Microsoft has since patched the PowerShell vulnerability , safely scoping the authentication mechanism to ensure that users’ tokens are only attached when a request host is an authorized GitHub endpoint, such as api.github.com , github.com , or raw.githubusercontent.com . Harush noted, however, that the underlying credential model is “fundamentally flawed,” and that relying on Classic PATs is a “severe liability.” Cycode advises binding credentials to destinations, rather than functions; auditing every internal tool that handles maintainer credentials; and ensuring that headers are conditionally applied based on the target host, “not unconditionally stapled by a wrapper function.” Treat all user inputs as hostile, validated hosts before credentials are attached, and deprecate classic PATs. “The blast radius of a leaked token must be limited to one repository and the bare minimum permissions,” Harush said. “A leaked token should never mean a leaked corporate identity.” He emphasized, though, that WinGet moderators are doing exactly what’s asked of them: Using automated tools to manage a “flood of community submissions” and make their jobs easier. “But automation does not just remove the human who would have clicked the malicious link; it removes the human who would have noticed the anomaly.” Scripts are a soft spot The WinGet flaw was a near miss, but “a very serious one,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. Exploiting it would have let an attacker publish malware with “Microsoft’s seal of approval.” This means attackers could have pushed tampered installers to anyone who ran an install or an update, reached into any other Microsoft repositories the moderator could touch, and hijacked the build machinery to steal more secrets. And the damage would have looked like routine work. An IT team scripting a standard software rollout would have installed the attacker’s code on every machine, and the logs would have shown an approved package from an approved source. “The attack would have been a Trojan horse delivered by the mail carrier everyone trusts,” Dickson said. Enterprise security teams should learn that their own scripts are a soft spot, he pointed out; internal tools, bots, and automation get production-level keys and hobby-level review. CISOs should inventory every script and bot that holds a token, and answer important questions: What could this key do in the wrong hands? Where is it allowed to go? Additionally, he advised replacing broad, long-lived tokens with narrow, short-lived ones, and binding every credential to the specific services that need it, which is exactly how Microsoft fixed this problem. “Also, enterprises should stop trusting public registries blindly,” Dickson said. Ultimately, security teams should review their automations the way they review their people, he said. “A script that runs in a loop around the clock with a moderator’s keys is, in effect, a moderator who never sleeps and never questions anything.”
summary: The most dangerous actor in a software supply chain may now be an automated script with powerful credentials and no idea where it’s sending them. Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet), which sits on billions of devices worldwide. A single pull request could have tricked Microsoft’s internal tooling into freely handing over a moderator’s GitHub access token, with no phishing, no malware, no moderator clicking or approval required. There is currently no evidence that the flaw has been exploited in the wild.

title: European Commission HR hit by cyber attack
raw_text: Barely a week after the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warned companies of the cyber attacker interest in an open source penetration testing tool called ARTEX, the European Commission has confirmed that attackers armed with that tool broke into its HR systems. The attack, which Commission officials detected on October 22, forced them to shut off much of the access to the systems for more than 10 days. “As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications and most of them have since then been restored,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Thursday. “We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole.” During a news media briefing, a transcript of which was provided to CSOonline, he said that the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) was informed of the attack, “so there was no hiding whatsoever.” Regnier would not go into detail about the attacks, given that the matter is still being investigated, but he did say, “it is a campaign, so there was a series of incidents.” In an email, Commission officials added, “we are also preventively checking other systems while staying in close contact with CERT-EU and the EDPS.” ARTEX popular with attackers The November 13 FBI statement about ARTEX, described as an autonomous penetration testing framework, said that the tool is becoming very popular with attackers. “Since at least August 2026, a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal industries,” the FBI advisory said. “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale.” Although ARTEX can handle a wide range of pentesting functions, it appeared to be primarily used in the Commission attack to search for and locate credentials. The FBI said that ARTEX can “automatically map effective permissions of Azure credentials–SAS tokens, Service Principals, Kudu credentials, Storage Account keys–using sub-second capability checks.” ARTEX has been known to SOC operations since GitHub first released the tool in July, but widespread misuse of the tool prompted GitHub to make it unavailable on October 8. “Despite this action, ARTEX remains widely accessible through independent routes and mirrors on code-sharing platforms,” the FBI said. Uses different tactics Brian Levine , a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, added that ARTEX’s AI-fueled tactics are different from what many cybersecurity teams are used to. “ARTEX doesn’t need to steal your keys. It finds the ones you left lying around, like a SAS token in a code repo, a storage key in a config file, or a Kudu credential nobody rotated. Then it tries each one against every door in under a second,” he said. “Picture a burglar walking the block at 3 a.m. and checking every car door handle. He isn’t breaking glass. He’s taking inventory of what you left unlocked and AI lets him work a thousand blocks at once.” Companies need a secure fallback Noah Kenney , principal consultant at Digital 520, said he was unimpressed with the Commission’s attempts to tell EU citizens that all was well. “The Commission says it has no evidence of a breach affecting its staff ‘as a whole,’ which is very different from saying that there is no evidence of a breach affecting any of the staff,” Kenney said. “The wording doesn’t give me much comfort.” Kenney also said that the attackers’ decision to target HR was not an accident, and that the Commission’s decision to temporarily shut down some systems may have inadvertently helped the intruders. “When payroll, leave, and medical reimbursement systems go down, people start using spreadsheets, email and manual approvals. Those workarounds often have weaker access controls and worse audit trails than the systems taken offline,” he said. “Enterprises need to define a secure fallback process before the attack, because improvising one often leads to greater exposure.” HR systems a prize Levine also said that the choice of an HR victim was understandable. “HR systems are a prize. Names, home addresses, pay grades and health insurance records for EU civil servants make a ready-made targeting list for espionage and social engineering,” he said. “Whether or not data left the building, every Commission employee should prepare to receive a very convincing phishing email soon.” His advice to CISOs: “Get secrets out of code and pipelines and rotate anything that has been exposed. Give every token and service principal only the access it needs, so a found key opens a closet, not the vault. Put cloud admin interfaces behind private access.”

title: Critical flaw in VMware vCenter allows authentication bypass
raw_text: Broadcom has released patches for bugs in multiple products, one of which, fixing a VMware vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, is rated 9.8 out of 10 in severity. The company’s advisory describes the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 , as “an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service,” that could let a threat actor with network access gain unauthorized access to the system, and says there are no workarounds. It advises immediate patching. Broadcom has provided fixed vCenter versions 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 U3m; customers running v7.0 will only get a patch if they have an extended support contract. The patched version of VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x is 5.2.5. Customers using the VMware Telco Cloud Platform and Infrastructure, also affected, should consult KB463116 for remediation instructions. The remaining four issues are: SDDC Manager SQL-injection vulnerability ( CVE-2026-123891 ), rated 8.1 (Important) in severity; SDDC Manager authenticated command-injection vulnerability ( CVE-2026-123892 ), rated 7.2 (Important); SDDC Manager local privilege-escalation vulnerability ( CVE-2026-123893 ), rated 6.7 (Moderate), and VMware Tools SAML Token Signature Bypass vulnerability ( CVE-2026-123894 ), also rated 6.7. There are no workarounds for any of them. Broadcom has released a supplementary FAQ providing addition information on all five bugs, in which it said, “You are affected if you are running any version of VMware vCenter, SDDC Manager, or VMware Tools for Windows prior to the versions listed as “fixed” in the [advisory]. This includes vCenter and SDDC Manager deployed standalone and as part of VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation, VMware Telco Cloud Platform, and VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure, as well as VMware Tools installed in Windows virtual machines.” This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld .
