title: Palo Alto Networks bets $4.5B on enterprise AI with Applied Compute acquisition
raw_text: Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion, a move the company said will let it train, deploy and secure open-weight AI models for enterprises in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments. “The acquisition will bring Applied Compute’s platform and world-class AI research team to Palo Alto Networks to help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both,” the company said in a statement released alongside its fiscal first quarter 2027 results. The statement described Applied Compute as “a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models” and said the startup will continue to serve AI-native companies, digital natives and large enterprises. The transaction is expected to close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027, which runs from February to April, the statement said. Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer, and the startup’s research team will help build AI models across the company’s offerings. A security company that wants to run models Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and CEO, said on the company’s earnings call that beyond building AI into its own security products, “we will help train and serve secure sovereign implementations of open-weight models to the enterprise.” “Open-weight model implementations will allow us to deliver secure, open-weight models to our customers to enable adoption of secure AI in the enterprise,” Arora said. He said open-weight models had grown from under 5% of token traffic to more than 60% over the past year, without saying where the figure came from. Asked by JP Morgan analyst Brian Essex about customer demand, Arora said deterministic security controls “cannot anticipate every scenario that an agent is going to conduct.” Enterprises building AI applications “will have to train a supervisory AI model at the same time,” he said, because Palo Alto cannot secure models it has no part in building. “I cannot go in and intercept and understand somebody else’s application,” he said. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said Arora has a point, since a generic filter cannot know how a particular application is meant to behave. But most failures in AI applications happen at runtime, through prompts, tools, and permissions, whoever trained the model, he said. He noted that Palo Alto has sold model-agnostic protection through Prisma AIRS since 2025. “A supervisor trained by the same hands as the system it supervises is a colleague, not a check,” Gogia said, adding that CIOs should make sure someone other than the trainer tests the result. GPUs and data centers To train and host those models, Palo Alto plans to build its own compute capacity, CFO Dipak Golechha said on the call. The spending “will mostly go to GPUs and servers,” with a smaller share for the facilities that house them, he said. Palo Alto will “continue to source from our cloud partners” and add dedicated capacity over time, Golechha said. Arora said the company aims for more than100 megawatts of compute in the next three to five years. Gogia said Palo Alto has sovereignty credentials for security data, including customer-held keys and a European Cortex service governed by Deutsche Telekom. “None of that yet extends to GPUs,” he said, adding that a US-headquartered operator faces the same jurisdictional questions as the hyperscalers it rents capacity from. “A sovereign hosting offer with no named region, operator or date is a promise looking for an address,” Gogia said. Compliance officers should ask Palo Alto for a region list, the operator, and a dated certification plan, he said. Arora said on the call that the training and inference business could eventually exceed Palo Alto’s core market. “This could be bigger than what we do today,” he said. One vendor, more of the stack The deal follows Palo Alto’s $25 billion purchase of CyberArk , which added identity security to its platform. Gogia said Applied Compute would now add the models themselves to a supplier already at the center of many customers’ firewalls, SOC, and identity controls. “Palo Alto is asking enterprises to let the guard build the vault it guards,” he said. One team watching both model and telemetry can spot trouble sooner, he said, but a single fault, breach or pricing dispute would land “on the protection and the protected together.” CIOs should get a costed exit in writing before any model work moves across, Gogia said. Applied Compute customers should use the months before closing to secure ownership of trained weights in an exportable format, no training on their data without consent, a right to exit on change of control and price protection that survives bundling, he said. “Terms are cheapest to win while the suitor is still courting,” Gogia said.
summary: Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion, a move the company said will let it train, deploy and secure open-weight AI models for enterprises in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments. “The acquisition will bring Applied Compute’s platform and world-class AI research team to Palo Alto Networks to help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both,” the company said in a statement released alongside its fiscal first quarter 2027 results. The statement described Applied Compute as “a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models” and said the startup will continue to serve AI-native companies, digital natives and large enterprises. The transaction is expected to close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027, which runs from February to April, the statement said.

title: Vulnerability management: The cybersecurity industry is still solving the wrong problem
raw_text: We have never been short of vulnerabilities. We have always struggled with remedial work. For decades, the cybersecurity industry has approached vulnerability management from the wrong end. The emphasis has consistently been on finding vulnerabilities, cataloguing them, scoring them and, more recently, prioritising them through increasingly sophisticated risk models. An entire industry has developed around vulnerability scanning, exposure management, threat intelligence and remediation prioritization. Artificial intelligence is now promising to take those capabilities to another level. But there is something fundamentally wrong with that approach. The real challenge in vulnerability management has never been identifying what needs fixing. It has always been getting the remedial work done. Most large organizations already know they have significant numbers of vulnerabilities across their technology estates. They have known for years. They have dashboards, reports, inventories, risk ratings and remediation backlogs. What they frequently lack is the organizational machinery to translate that knowledge into effective, sustained remedial action. And that is not primarily a technology problem. The uncomfortable reality behind remediation backlogs Consider what happens when a large enterprise identifies a critical vulnerability. The security team assesses its severity and potential impact. It raises a ticket, assigns a priority, identifies an owner and requests remediation. On paper, the process looks straightforward. In practice, that is often where the real problems begin. The infrastructure team may be managing ageing systems with complex dependencies. The development team may have committed to a demanding release schedule. Production operations may be unwilling to accept additional downtime. Business stakeholders may resist disruption to revenue-generating services. Some systems may have very limited maintenance windows. Others may require extensive regression testing before deploying patches. Legacy applications may depend on components that cannot easily be upgraded. And ownership itself may be disputed. Security teams frequently have the responsibility to identify and report vulnerabilities but lack the authority to enforce remediation. Technology teams control the systems but may have competing priorities and insufficient resources. The result is familiar: escalating tickets, repeated exceptions, missed deadlines, unresolved disputes and growing remediation backlogs. None of these problems can be solved simply by producing a better vulnerability score. Prioritization is necessary, but it is not the answer The industry has increasingly recognized that organizations cannot remediate everything. That has driven the development of risk-based vulnerability management, exploitability intelligence, asset criticality models and sophisticated exposure prioritization platforms. These capabilities have genuine value: There is an obvious difference between a vulnerability that is actively exploited on an internet-facing critical system and one that exists on an isolated, low-value asset. But prioritization is only the beginning of a management process. It is not its outcome: A perfectly prioritized remediation backlog remains a backlog. In many organizations, the difficulty is not deciding which vulnerabilities matter most. It is securing agreement on who will fix them, when the work will take place and who has the authority to resolve conflicts or accept the risk. These are matters of governance, accountability and business priorities. The cybersecurity industry remains disproportionately focused on the what , when the real challenge lies in the how and the who . AI is about to make the problem considerably worse Artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing the economics of vulnerability discovery. AI-assisted tools can analyse code, identify weaknesses and accelerate vulnerability research on a scale and at a speed that would previously have required substantial human effort. According to Google Threat Intelligence Group , monthly vulnerability disclosures more than doubled between January and August 2026, while observed exploitation also increased significantly. AI is contributing to that acceleration, although changes in disclosure practices also influence the figures. The consequences for large organizations could be significant. We are moving towards a world where the identification of vulnerabilities becomes increasingly automated, increasingly inexpensive and potentially continuous. But what happens when the volume of identified vulnerabilities increases dramatically while the organization’s capacity to remediate them remains essentially unchanged? The answer is predictable: Larger backlogs. More pressure on technology teams. More exceptions. More disputes over priorities. And potentially greater exposure, despite unprecedented visibility into technical weaknesses. The Cloud Security Alliance has already highlighted this growing disconnect between accelerated vulnerability discovery and the capacity of organizations to absorb and remediate findings. AI is industrialising vulnerability discovery while remediation remains trapped in organizational structures designed for another era. That is the real emerging challenge. AI cannot negotiate a production maintenance window Of course, AI can also contribute to remediation. It can establish proofs of concept, generate and test fixes, propose configuration changes, analyse dependencies and automate certain deployment activities. These are important developments, and organizations should embrace them where appropriate. But their practical impact must not be overstated. AI cannot independently decide that a critical production system should be taken offline during a peak business period. It cannot assume accountability for disrupting customer services or resolve competing priorities between a business unit, an infrastructure team and the security function. It cannot simply override legacy dependencies, contractual obligations or regulatory constraints. Even where AI can technically generate a suitable fix, somebody still needs to validate it, approve its deployment, ensure that the fix has not broken something else and verify that remediation has been successful. Some of those steps can be automated. Others require judgement, authority and organizational coordination. The more powerful AI becomes, the more visible those remaining management bottlenecks will be. And this is where the traditional cybersecurity approach is increasingly inadequate. Vulnerability management needs an operating model, not another dashboard What large organizations need is not simply better vulnerability management technology. They need a remediation operating model that establishes clear accountability across security, development, infrastructure, operations and business management. That model should address several fundamental questions. Who owns the remediation of vulnerabilities affecting shared platforms or complex applications? Who allocates the necessary resources? Who can authorize emergency changes? Who resolves disagreements when remediation conflicts with business priorities? How are maintenance windows negotiated and secured? How are persistent exceptions challenged? Who accepts the residual business risk when remediation cannot be completed within the expected timeframe? And, crucially, who is responsible for ensuring that agreed actions happen? These responsibilities cannot be left to informal relationships between technical teams or to the persistence of individual security managers. They need to be embedded in management processes, supported by executive authority and reinforced through meaningful performance measures. Security should provide risk intelligence, challenge and assurance. Technology teams should own the delivery of remediation within their environments. Business management should participate in decisions where operational disruption or investment trade-offs are unavoidable. The CISO’s role is to help establish and oversee that machinery, not to become the organization’s chief ticket chaser. Measuring remediation effectiveness, not just reporting activity There is also a fundamental problem with how vulnerability management performance is measured. Too many organizations remain focused on the number of vulnerabilities identified, severity distributions, compliance with remediation deadlines and the volume of outstanding findings. Those indicators have their place, but they can encourage an administrative approach to vulnerability management: Closing tickets becomes a proxy for reducing risk. What matters is whether material exposures are being eliminated within acceptable timeframes and whether the organization can demonstrate that remediation has worked. Management should pay particular attention to recurring remediation failures, ageing high-risk exposures, operational bottlenecks, the effectiveness of exception handling and the time required to implement verified fixes. The distinction between a vulnerability being reported as resolved and genuinely being remediated is essential. AI can help generate more accurate and timely evidence. But it cannot substitute for accountability over the results. Auditability and regulatory obligations add another critical dimension to this challenge. Regulators increasingly expect organizations not only to identify and assess vulnerabilities, but also to demonstrate that appropriate remedial actions have been taken within reasonable timeframes. This requires clear ownership, documented decisions, traceable exceptions periodically reviewed and reliable evidence that remediation has been completed. As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and potentially automates parts of the remediation process, maintaining an auditable chain of accountability becomes even more important. Ultimately, compliance cannot rest on the ability to identify problems: It needs to rest on the ability to demonstrate that they have been effectively addressed . The real opportunity for AI is to transform execution This is where I believe the cybersecurity industry should concentrate its attention. Rather than simply applying AI to discover more vulnerabilities and refine their prioritization or their treatment, vendors and practitioners should focus on how AI can accelerate the entire remediation lifecycle. That means understanding dependencies, identifying suitable deployment opportunities, preparing changes, automating testing, coordinating workflows, validating results and providing management with reliable evidence of progress across the whole cycle. In highly automated environments, AI agents may eventually execute substantial portions of that process under clearly defined controls. But the objective should not be automation for its own sake: It should be to reduce the friction between identifying a problem and resolving it. And that requires technology to be designed around a functioning governance model, rather than expecting governance to emerge from the technology. The technology will change. The management problem will not. I have argued for years that cybersecurity is fundamentally a leadership and management challenge supported by technology. Vulnerability management provides perhaps one of the clearest demonstrations of that principle. The same structural problems that prevented organizations from patching critical systems fifteen years ago remain visible today: fragmented responsibilities, competing priorities, operational constraints, weak governance and insufficient management follow-through. AI will not make those problems disappear. On the contrary, by accelerating vulnerability discovery and shortening the time available to respond, it is exposing them more brutally than ever. The organizations that succeed will not necessarily be those with the most sophisticated vulnerability discovery capabilities. They will be those that have built the governance, accountability and operational discipline required to translate technical intelligence into effective remedial action. The future of vulnerability management will not be determined by how quickly we can find what is wrong. It will be determined by how effectively organizations can get things fixed. And that has always been a management problem.
summary: We have never been short of vulnerabilities. We have always struggled with remedial work. For decades, the cybersecurity industry has approached vulnerability management from the wrong end. The emphasis has consistently been on finding vulnerabilities, cataloguing them, scoring them and, more recently, prioritising them through increasingly sophisticated risk models.

title: AI unearths ‘internet breaker’ flaws in Nginx web server
raw_text: Nginx, the web server estimated to power a third of the internet, has shipped fixes for multiple vulnerabilities, including a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw that puts millions of websites at risk and has existed in the code for over a decade. Researchers from several security firms independently found some of the same flaws by using AI agents, adding to a string of recent AI-discovered vulnerabilities in widely used internet technologies such as PHP, Node, OpenSSH, and Java. The most severe flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an attacker manipulate flow-control windows in the HTTP/2 protocol implementation to trigger an out-of-bounds memory copy that researchers from Xint.io turned into command execution with Nginx worker privileges . The vulnerability affects every official Nginx release for more than 10 years since version 1.9.5, which originally added HTTP/2 support in 2015. A second HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-123633, is a use-after-free vulnerability affecting releases 1.19.7 through 1.31.8. Both are fixed in Nginx 1.31.9 and 1.30.7, which F5 released along with fixes for eight other vulnerabilities. Xint’s researchers, who used the company’s own autonomous AI harness, found five of the flaws and discovered a separate Linux kernel vulnerability in the SCTP subsystem that can be chained with any of those flaws to gain root privileges on the server. The company has dubbed the collection nginx2root . In their tests the exploit chain escaped a Docker container running Nginx and obtained root on the underlying host. The kernel flaw has existed since Linux 4.15, released in 2018, and has no CVE or patch so the company is withholding details until distributions can ship a fix. The exposure of web servers on the internet is vast with the Shodan search engine showing 56.7 million hosts running Nginx, and 98.9% of those that disclose their version report one in the vulnerable range. F5 recommends updating immediately or disabling HTTP/2 on affected ports, which blocks the two most severe flaws but not Xint’s other findings — CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, and CVE-2026-113425 — which are in other components. The CVE-2026-123007 flaw was reported to F5 by researchers from Rapid7 , Wiz , Xint, and Ikotas Labs , while CVE-2026-123633, dubbed Drainbreak, was discovered and reported by researchers from Metnir , Wiz, and Xint. Only Rapid7 senior principal security researcher Stephen Fewer doesn’t mention AI in his write-up. The other four teams used AI agents and harnesses, with Xint’s CEO Brian Pak saying that his team’s platform scanned “50,000 lines of code in just 90 minutes” to surface “a critical vulnerability that gave an unauthenticated user a RCE path — essentially an internet breaker.” Exploitation is likely No one has exploited either flaw in the wild yet, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s assessment of both CVEs, but every research team built working exploits, and two describe the flaws as readily exploitable. Xint called CVE-2026-123007 highly exploitable, saying an externally reachable TLS/HTTP/2 port was enough to corrupt the send window, disclose addresses, and execute commands, and validated the attack over public IPs on AWS, GCP, and Azure under concurrent traffic. Metnir ran its exploit for CVE-2026-123633 with ASLR enabled, taking about 10 minutes, nearly all of it spent on defeating memory layout randomization, and reproduced the use-after-free in OpenResty, crashing the shipped binaries of Kong, Apache APISIX, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and community ingress-nginx, all of which enable HTTP/2 by default. Rapid7’s Fewer calculated that running his exploit requires transmitting roughly 128GB of HTTP/2 data to the target. That takes about two minutes on a 10Gbit/s network and 17 minutes on 1Gbit/s. The technique also relies on a memory-copy routine in glibc that is used only on CPUs with AVX-512 extensions, but these are common on servers. “Exploitation is by no means a walk in the park, as the vulnerable systems must be directly exposed to the internet with no WAF or CDN terminating HTTP/2,” Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, told CSO. “Memory corruption can also be tricky, as an effective exploit must properly groom and shape the memory heap and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configuration variants. And when the system is internet-facing and under load, exploitation can cause more crashes than successful code execution.” Patch and check what you’re actually running Nginx Plus users should also update to 37.3.0.1 on the newer release line or 37.0.8.1 on the 37.0 line. The older R33 through R36 release line will never receive a fix because those versions have reached the end of technical support. Disabling HTTP/2 comes with costs, as services that depend on it, such as native gRPC, stop working. Xint’s other three flaws require specific configurations. The resolver flaw affects setups that pick their backend per request and use the mirror directive, the HTTP/3 flaw affects QUIC listeners, and the mail proxy flaw affects deployments that use proxy on with auth_http . Xint published per-flaw mitigations in its technical write-up. For the accompanying Linux flaw, until a kernel patch is released, administrators who don’t use SCTP can block the module from loading by adding install sctp /bin/false to a file under /etc/modprobe.d . Administrators should also investigate unexpected Nginx worker crashes or commands launched by Nginx workers, Wiz noted. “The real risk with this nginx bug isn’t the 11 years it went unnoticed, it’s how many teams will think they’ve patched when they haven’t,” Daniel Shechter, co-founder and CEO of Miggo Security, told CSO. “The version number can be wrong because distros backport fixes without changing it, a reload doesn’t swap out the running code, and the attack happens in HTTP/2 traffic that WAFs and access logs never see. If you can’t prove the fix is actually running, assume you’re still exposed.”
summary: Nginx, the web server estimated to power a third of the internet, has shipped fixes for multiple vulnerabilities, including a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw that puts millions of websites at risk and has existed in the code for over a decade. Researchers from several security firms independently found some of the same flaws by using AI agents, adding to a string of recent AI-discovered vulnerabilities in widely used internet technologies such as PHP, Node, OpenSSH, and Java. The most severe flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an attacker manipulate flow-control windows in the HTTP/2 protocol implementation to trigger an out-of-bounds memory copy that researchers from Xint.io turned into command execution with Nginx worker privileges . The vulnerability affects every official Nginx release for more than 10 years since version 1.9.5, which originally added HTTP/2 support in 2015.

title: A new critical Java hole illustrates the enterprise IT visibility problem
raw_text: When cybersecurity research firm Calif published details Tuesday of a potentially major Java security flaw, dubbed Java4Shell, it described an unauthenticated attacker’s ability to read Java heap memory, steal private keys, tokens, and session secrets, and reach remote code execution (RCE). With Java being all-but-ubiquitous in today’s enterprise, coupled with the inability of CISOs to have visibility into every instance of it in their estate, this means that the bug could be a big problem for IT. Java, which has had its fair share of cybersecurity issues lately, is well-known for safely handling memory. That is why a Java bug affecting memory management is so dangerous. Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 , is a vulnerability in the OpenJDK x86-64 Base64 decoder that scores 9.2 in severity (Critical) under CVSS 4.0, Calif said. Oracle assigned it a lower rating of 8.1 (High) using CVSS 3.1. Calif explained in its post describing the issue that Base64 is a common way of representing binary data as text. “It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” it wrote. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution.” It said that the corruption can be triggered by a string of just 64 “A” characters followed by a single equals sign (=); in older OpenJDK 17 versions, 128 “A” characters are required before the equals sign. “Memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the internet,” Calif said. “But one of Java’s biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers’ behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software. But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life.” Assessing the bug’s potential for exploit is complicated because triggering it requires a hardware accelerated decoding function that’s used on some x86-64 processors supporting AVX-512 VBMI instructions. And fixing it requires patches from a lengthy list of vendors; just installing Tuesday’s patch from Oracle, which owns Java, is not going to do the trick. Potential damage ‘extreme’ Noah Kenney , principal consultant at Digital 520, said the potential damage from an unpatched instance of exposed Java is extreme. “The researchers were able to read Java heap memory before they achieved code execution, so an attacker may be able to steal tokens, credentials, or keys from those systems. That access can remain useful even after the vulnerable server has been patched,” Kenney said. “Any unexplained crashes on an exposed system should lead to a review of what secrets were in memory and whether they need to be rotated.” But not every instance is vulnerable to this flaw. “The same Java application and version can be vulnerable on a newer x86 server and unaffected on older hardware because the faulty decoder only runs when AVX-512 is available,” he noted. “That makes a normal software inventory less useful than it usually is. CISOs need to know the Java distribution and version, the processor underneath it, and whether untrusted Base64 reaches the decoder. Installing a newer processor can expose an application that was safe on the server it replaced, without changing the application at all.” A further complication is that enterprises will also be running Java from a massive array of specialized vendors. “Oracle released a fix for its Java builds, but enterprises also run Java from Amazon, Eclipse, Microsoft, Red Hat, and Azul, along with runtimes buried inside commercial products and containers,” Kenney pointed out. “CISOs should start with identity systems and software-delivery infrastructure, identify the runtime each one is actually using, apply the appropriate vendor fix, and restart or rebuild the workload.” He also said that outbound connections need to be evaluated. “Researchers demonstrated that a Java program could be compromised by connecting to a malicious TLS server, even when it had no service exposed to the internet.” Aman Mahapatra , chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, agreed, pointing out, “the client-side exploit puts any Java process that connects to a malicious TLS server at risk: integrations, connectors, crawlers and batch jobs. Patch scopes built around internet-facing listeners will miss them.” Lack of visibility a big problem Mahapatra also stressed that many Java implementations can be hard to locate. “Your SBOM [software bill of materials] can’t see the real exposure. Whether a service is vulnerable depends on the silicon underneath as much as the JDK version,” he said. “The same container image is exploitable on an Ice Lake or Zen 4 node and safe on ARM or older hardware, and autoscaling can move it between the two. For once, the organizations that refreshed their hardware are the exposed ones.” But it is the lack of visibility that concerns practitioners the most. The Java hole “exposes a blind spot in how enterprises identify, prioritize and validate vulnerabilities,” said Raj Annaladasu , staff customer success engineer at Palo Alto Networks. “Enterprise teams invest heavily in application code review, dependency scanning, and secure coding practices. Java4Shell is a reminder that vulnerabilities can originate below the application layer, inside the managed runtime itself.” “This is an important distinction: Java’s memory-safety abstractions do not protect an application from memory corruption originating inside a vulnerable native runtime implementation,” he said. “Applications may be using a standard Java API correctly while the underlying runtime implementation is vulnerable. This shifts the security boundary beyond application code and third-party dependencies to include the runtime, its implementation, and the hardware capabilities that influence execution.” This means, he said, that exploitability depends on multiple conditions coming together: an affected Java runtime, the relevant CPU instruction capabilities, the vulnerable execution path being enabled, and attacker-controlled input reaching the decoder. But, he pointed out, “one of the bigger challenges is discovering where Java is actually running. Runtime installations are often bundled inside third-party products, container images, appliances, custom runtime distributions, and application-specific directories. They may not appear as distinct entries in conventional software inventories. A clean application dependency scan or CMDB does not establish that the environment is free of vulnerable Java runtimes.” Java hides everywhere Given that there are going to be so many Java vendors, and so many hidden apps, at issue, the risk of a CISO missing a few is massive, noted Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research. “Java4Shell is a big deal because a single missed server with Java is all an attacker needs, allowing someone who never logs in to read its memory, including personal data, private keys, and tokens,” he said. “From there, the attacker can run code on the server. If that server is an identity system like Keycloak or PingFederate, the attacker now owns you.” And, he said, it’s highly unlikely that enterprise CISOs will catch all or most Java instances. “Will a CISO miss one? The odds say yes. Java hides everywhere. Each Java instance needs its own fix,” Dickson said. Its popularity is Java’s greatest weakness Brian Levine , a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, said Java’s popularity is its biggest weakness. “Java runs the back office of corporate America: logins, code pipelines, ticketing, internal wikis,” he said. “Java4Shell lets an attacker who hasn’t even logged in take over some of the most sensitive of those systems by sending a short string of text. If your company runs Java on modern servers, and almost every large company does, you’re exposed until you patch.” He enumerated some examples: “Keycloak and PingFederate control who gets into your company. Jenkins and Artifactory build and store the software you ship. Jira and Confluence hold your roadmaps, incident notes and plenty of passwords people shouldn’t have pasted there,” he said. “Take over those and you aren’t breaking into one room. You’ve stolen the master key, the blueprints and the security guard’s notebook in one move.” He added, “Java programs that simply connect out to the wrong server can be compromised too. That last one means firewalls and perimeter controls don’t fully protect you.” However, he pointed out, “there’s one small mercy: the bug only fires on certain newer Intel and AMD chips. The catch is that those chips fill modern data centers and cloud fleets.”
summary: When cybersecurity research firm Calif published details Tuesday of a potentially major Java security flaw, dubbed Java4Shell, it described an unauthenticated attacker’s ability to read Java heap memory, steal private keys, tokens, and session secrets, and reach remote code execution (RCE). With Java being all-but-ubiquitous in today’s enterprise, coupled with the inability of CISOs to have visibility into every instance of it in their estate, this means that the bug could be a big problem for IT. Java, which has had its fair share of cybersecurity issues lately, is well-known for safely handling memory. That is why a Java bug affecting memory management is so dangerous.

title: OX Security Launches OX Radar and Response Center to Show Companies Which Cyber Threats Actually Affect Them
raw_text: New technology monitors critical vulnerabilities and supply chain threats, automatically assessing customer exposure and guiding remediation OX Security , a leader in AI-native application protection, today announced the launch of OX Radar and Response Center, giving security teams one place to track high-priority cyber threats, determine whether their organizations are affected, and manage remediation. OX Radar continuously monitors emerging vulnerabilities, compromised software dependencies, and actively exploited threats. Integrated with OX Security’s application security platform, the Response Center automatically checks supported threats against customer environments, identifying affected assets and providing the context and guidance needed to respond. Separately, a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed provides broader security research and findings across the software and AI supply chain. When a major vulnerability or supply chain attack emerges, security teams often spend hours searching advisories, checking inventories, and correlating findings across tools to answer the question that matters most: Are we affected? As new software and AI components proliferate, investigating every potential threat manually is becoming increasingly impractical. “The question isn’t just whether a new threat is dangerous. It’s whether it’s dangerous to you,” said Neatsun Ziv, CEO and co-founder of OX Security. “AI is accelerating software development, expanding the supply chain, and generating more security alerts than teams can realistically investigate. Security teams need to know immediately which threats affect their organization, which don’t, and what action is required.” From Breaking Threats to Customer Action To help security teams stay ahead of threats requiring urgent attention, OX Radar scans CVE databases, known-exploited vulnerability catalogs, security advisories, and vendor research approximately every 10 minutes. The customer-facing capabilities focus on high-priority threats, including compromised or malicious dependencies, exploited vulnerabilities, and critical-severity CVEs. The Response Center connects supported OX Radar threats to each customer’s environment, checking whether vulnerable components are present and assessing their exploitability. It combines intelligence from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, EPSS exploit predictions, and VEX exploitability status with OX Security’s AI-generated exploit checks and runtime visibility to determine whether vulnerable libraries are affected. Through the Response Center, security teams can: Track threats: Follow high-priority incidents as new intelligence and findings emerge. Assess exposure: Identify affected assets and examine supporting evidence. Prioritize risk: Evaluate severity, exploitation, code usage, and reachability. Manage remediation: Access safe versions and guidance, and create or track tickets and fix pull requests. Document response: Maintain records of findings and remediation activity. For each supported incident, the Response Center indicates whether a vulnerability has been detected in the customer’s environment, provides evidence of its potential exploitability, and incorporates available VEX information to help teams determine whether action is required. Teams can also initiate investigations using a CVE identifier, GitHub Security Advisory identifier, or advisory URL. Expanding Threat Visibility Through Public Research Alongside the customer-facing capabilities, OX Security is introducing a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed with a broader catalog of security findings. Powered by OX Security’s independent research and scanning, the feed analyzes newly published npm and PyPI packages, AI skills, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. OX Security will continue expanding the range of threats assessed against customer environments, bringing more findings from its public research into the Response Center over time. Availability OX Radar and Response Center are available to OX Security customers as part of OX Security’s AI-Native Application Protection Platform (AINAPP). The broader OX Radar research feed is publicly accessible through the OX Security website. About OX Security OX Security is the first AI-Native Application Protection Platform built to secure software from prompt to production runtime. Its platform includes VibeSec, OX Code, OX Cloud, and OX Agentic Pentester, giving security teams a unified system for securing AI-driven development, applications, and cloud environments. Contact Head of Communications Jillian Jones OX Security jillian.jones@ox.security

OX Radar continuously monitors emerging vulnerabilities, compromised software dependencies, and actively exploited threats. Integrated with OX Security’s application security platform, the Response Center automatically checks supported threats against customer environments, identifying affected assets and providing the context and guidance needed to respond. Separately, a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed provides broader security research and findings across the software and AI supply chain.

title: Attackers hijack Microsoft’s agent-framework package to steal Azure and CI credentials
raw_text: Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft’s official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers. Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour. “The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post . The payload ran automatically every time Python started, even if no code imported the package, OX said. The malicious versions also installed the genuine framework code, so applications kept working, and the compromise was easy to miss. The package has 192,534 monthly downloads, according to the firm. Other security firms, including Aikido Security, Endor Labs, and SafeDep, published similar analyses of the attack. Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. How the stealer worked The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said. It also read up to 60 credential files. These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files. It pulled secrets from up to 300 other running processes as well. The stealer also asked for new tokens. Inside Azure DevOps pipelines, it requested an identity token that can be exchanged for Azure access, OX said in the blog post. It also requested managed identity tokens for Azure services, including Resource Manager, Microsoft Graph, Key Vault, Storage, Cognitive Services, AI Foundry, and Azure DevOps. Endor Labs said the attack was aimed mainly at automated build systems. “Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis . The code was disguised as diagnostics. It sat in a module named _telemetry.py and sent data with a user agent labeled “af-runtime-diagnostics,” OX said. The stolen data went to a webhook.site address as compressed, encoded JSON. The attacker did not stop after the first release. While OX was researching the malware, version 1.26.1 was reverted to the clean 1.26.0. The attacker then uploaded 1.26.2, which used a different file path for the same payload, the firm said. The first version went up at 20:35 UTC and the second at 21:08 UTC, according to Aikido Security . Both were gone by about 21:20 UTC. “This attack isn’t just a one-off exfiltration attempt, but a planned, live and coordinated effort to reach as many victims as they can, while still being able to bypass blocks and restrictions,” OX said. OX said the attackers appear to have found a way to hijack the process that builds the package’s wheel files. Endor Labs, in its analysis, said both malicious versions were uploaded as wheel files only, without the source code package that came with the clean release. Microsoft has not confirmed how the breach happened. The short window may not limit exposure. Any unpinned install during that time pulled in a malicious version, Endor Labs said. Container images, CI caches, and lockfiles built in the window could still contain it. AI pipelines in focus OX said the attack shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it. The stealer’s target list includes OpenAI and Hugging Face tokens and Azure AI Foundry access. It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions. No researcher has linked the two attacks. What security teams should do Removing the package does not undo the damage. “Removing the package stops future runs, but it doesn’t undo anything that was already sent,” Aikido said. OX advised teams to check all environments, CI images, and lockfiles for either version and remove it. Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said. Version 1.26.2 used different files, af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py, according to Aikido. If the package ran anywhere, every secret reachable from that host should be treated as compromised, OX said. The firm recommended rotating Azure service principal secrets, personal access tokens, and GitHub, npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI tokens. OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents. Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.
summary: Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft’s official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers. Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour. “The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post . The payload ran automatically every time Python started, even if no code imported the package, OX said.

title: AI red team tool Artex likely behind cyber attack on EU body
raw_text:
Artex, an open-source AI-powered penetration-testing framework, may have been implicated in a cyber incident affecting the European Union’s (EU’s) executive body, the European Commission (EC) in Brussels.

The attack, which unfolded at the end of October, appears to have targeted the Commision’s Sysper human resources (HR) platform, leaving staffers unable to undertake some key tasks. The EC swiftly took down affected systems and Computer Weekly understands Sysper is back online at the time of writing, although according to Euronews other systems – including a health insurance programme – are still offline.

Speaking on Thursday 19 November, Commission spokesperson for digital Thomas Regnier said: “The investigation is still ongoing. We are taking any necessary steps based on the findings as they come…. We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole.”

The European Union’s (EU’s) Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said: “CERT-EU has observed similar instances of AI-driven activities against its constituency. These activities highly likely involved the use of Artex.”

ISACA chief global strategy officer Chris Dimitriadis said: “On the eve of the EU-UK summit, the news that the European Commission has suffered a significant cyber attack exposes Europe’s executive body. 

 "While alarming, this attack is not surprising. Thanks to AI, attackers now hack at the speed of intent – a pace the public and private sector cannot outrun without serious investment in the cyber workforce. Until organisations deploy AI defensively as fast as criminals deploy it aggressively, we will continue on this trajectory. 

“In the short term, the Commission will investigate whether staff data has been compromised and what weakness hackers were able to use Artex to exploit. They should be bolstering their cyber security and building long-term resilience by investing in recruiting, training, and upskilling privacy professionals who can build defences that are stronger than the AI tools now freely available to attackers.” 

What is Artex?

At its core, the legitimate Artex framework consists of a large language model (LLM)-powered agentic platform, written in Go with a Next.js frontend.

It can be used to automate offensive cyber tasks and was recently identified by threat intel teams and law enforcement agencies as increasingly finding favour among cyber criminals thanks to its ability to shrink the time needed to chain various offensive cyber tasks.

Indeed, some intrusions orchestrated using Artex are believed to have moved from initial targeting to full privileged access in less than three hours, moving up cyber attack timelines.

But its value to a threat actor lies in not just its speed, but its scale and persistence as well. Artex is able to probe huge numbers of low-complexity issues, such as misconfigurations, that human eyes would miss, and of course it does not get tired or need tea breaks.

Microsoft said that the tool was being heavily used by a Chinese state-aligned threat actor tracked as Storm-0940, which has used Artex to obtain access to its victims’ cloud infrastructure – including Microsoft 365 environments. Redmond’s findings have been corroborated by Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and its Mandiant stablemate.

Artex was first released on GitHub by a user known by the handle Autumn-27 in July of this year and reached between 1,500 and 2,000 users in the space of 10 weeks, according to the FBI in the US.

Autumn-27 had allegedly stated that Artex was supposed to be used for “authorised security testing” within defined scopes, and in fact pulled its repository on 8 October after reports it was being abused.

Despite this, Artex persists and continues to proliferate through community forks, localised variants, and a commercial version, Artex Pro.

CERT-EU said: “We assess that Artex’s public availability will likely accelerate adoption by threat actors, resulting in more frequent, faster, and more scalable automated attacks with a higher success rate.”

“In April 2026, in our blog post AI is changing the economics of vulnerability discovery, we warned that autonomous offensive capabilities would progressively reach a wider range of actors. Artex is a concrete example of that shift materialising.”

Urgent steps for cyber teams

For security teams, CERT-EU has made available a list of tasks to undertake to safeguard against Artex.

In the immediate future, priorities should be to audit publicly exposed IT assets and limit exposure; to ensure management and control panels are isolated from the public internet or untrusted networks; to priorities emergency patching for all assets that must be exposed to the internet; and to monitor privileged and admin account activity for evidence of suspicious behaviour or abuse.

In the short-term, security teams should beef up their use of multifactor authentication (MFA), and hunt for and alert on connections to known or suspected threat infrastructure to identify potential compromises, particularly artefacts and behaviours consistent with Artex. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools can also be pressed into service to block strange processes.

On a continuous basis, security teams should sanitise error responses from internet-exposed devices to minimise threat actor enumeration of their assets, protect said assets with web application firewalls (WAFs), adopt detection and logging best practice for incident response, ensure monitoring covers AI tools and assets using them, conduct regular vulnerability scans and penetration tests, and retain all findings – even those that don’t seem very severe – in the remediation cycle, which can help stop tools like Artex from chaining a series of minor problems into a great big one.

What next for Artex?

Looking ahead, Snehal Antani, CEO of Horizon3, said the clear jump in attack volume and velocity seen in recent weeks was likely attributable to frameworks like Artex and similar tools than enable bad actors to harness fleets of agents, essentially industrialising cyber attacks using proven, basic techniques.

“Artex and the forks that followed it are the multiplier. One operator can now run many targets in parallel, and the agents keep iterating even when the human walks away,” said Antani.

In emailed comments, Antani told Computer Weekly that Artex and similar frameworks will drive a type of attack standardisation that makes attribution much harder.

“When different groups – state-aligned or purely criminal – are all running near-identical agent harnesses, models, and playbooks, their operational fingerprints start to look the same. You lose a lot of the traditional signals that used to separate actors.

“Going forward, expect this to become normal rather than exceptional. The skill barrier keeps dropping, the tooling keeps forking, and the economics favour volume. Organisations have significant cyber debt that is easily exploitable by frameworks like Artex, so we should expect persistent disruption of digital services – travel, banking, commerce, etcetera – in the coming months as these organisations scramble to quickly improve their cyber resilience.”

Antani warned that any defenders still inclined to treat exposure management as a quarterly scanning or annual penetration testing exercise will find themselves swiftly overwhelmed.

“Machine-speed offence is already here; machine-speed defence has to match it,” he said.

  • In a worst-case scenario, self-replicating artificial intelligence could launch cyber attacks at will against UK targets by 2028.
  • Anthropic’s revelation that a model broke out of its test environment three times and accessed external systems shows the power of these models.

title: Over 250,000 Londoners affected by latest TfL breach
raw_text:
The personal information of approximately 265,000 bus, rail and tube passengers in London has been exposed in a new data breach at service operator Transport for London (TfL).

The data leak affected users of TfL’s Oyster photocards – which are provided to children and students, the over-60s, military veterans and people participating in apprenticeship schemes, among other things.

It is understood to include names, email and home addresses, phone numbers, birthdates and security questions, but not photos, passwords, financial details, or data relating to journeys made on London’s transport network.

TfL technology strategy and revenue director Shashi Verma said: “The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologise to our customers affected by this incident.”

TfL has taken the photocard system offline to prevent any malicious access and reported the incident to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO). Affected users have also been contacted. It hopes to restore the service as soon as possible.

Speaking to the BBC, Verma revealed the breach came to light on Monday 16 November when photocard users received unexpected emails asking them to validate their TfL accounts, prompting an internal investigation.

In a statement, Verma said that the speed with which TfL had identified and closed down the attack meant its impact was more limited than it might otherwise have been.

He added that the compromised system had been subject to cyber security testing within the past 12 months, and pointed to the extensive work done in this regard following the 2024 Scattered Spider attack on its systems – for which two men were jailed earlier this year.

At the same time, he acknowledged that new hacking tools and techniques keep bubbling up, more so now than ever. “This is a very difficult game to keep up with,” he said.

Muhammad Yahya Patel, virtual chief information security officer (vCISO) and cyber security advisor for EMEA at Huntress, said: “265,000 people woke up to find their personal details in someone else’s hands through no fault of their own. Names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth and security question answers.

“That last one matters more than most people realise. Security questions are reused across multiple accounts. Someone who knows your mother’s maiden name or your first pet now potentially has a key that works on more than just your Oyster account.”

Patel praised TfL for taking the system offline quickly, and said the fact that financial data or journey histories had not been compromised was good news.

Vulnerable targets

Although TfL has stated no data on any children was compromised in the latest incident, Comparitech security specialist Brian Higgins said the breach was significant because it included the data of more potentially vulnerable people, such as young adults who recently left foster care, and elderly people.

“It’s vital they understand how to protect themselves after a breach like this and TfL has a duty of care to ensure that they receive the best advice as swiftly as possible, especially since this has happened before,” said Higgins.

“Some well-publicised, customer-facing aftercare would help in this case, regardless of culpability. The US started enforcing financial sanctions paid to victims in data breaches many years ago. Perhaps the ICO should consider such measures in the UK, especially where incidents involving a finite and manageable victim pool like this present themselves. A little more data protection stick than carrot might shrink our digital attack surface,” said Higgins.

Patel added: “Public services hold significant volumes of personal data on millions of people, and the security investment protecting that data needs to match the trust citizens place in those services. TfL has been a cyber attack target before. The question the ICO will be asking is whether the lessons from previous incidents translated into the controls that should have made this one harder to execute.” 

Next steps

Oyster photocard users are being advised to change their login details and security questions immediately, and if those details have been used on any other online services, to rotate those credentials as well.

Users should also be on the lookout for suspicious contacts by email, phone or SMS in the coming days and weeks.

“If you hold an Oyster photocard, treat any unexpected contact referencing your account, your address, or your personal details with immediate suspicion regardless of how official it looks,” said Patel.

While the photocard system remains offline for the time being, users who need to renew their photocards imminently can reach out to TfL by telephone on 0343 222 1234.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) also produces guidance for individuals and families caught up in an incident, available here.

Read more about recent UK data breaches

  • Following a data breach earlier in October, cyber criminals appear to have a much more complete picture of Asos’ user base than first thought, it has emerged.
  • The UK’s Department for Education has disclosed a serious data breach orchestrated via a social engineering attack on its external-facing helpdesk.
  • A data breach affecting 138 members of the Civil Service Pension Scheme piles pressure on the service’s administrator, Capita, amid ongoing issues.
summary:
The personal information of approximately 265,000 bus, rail and tube passengers in London has been exposed in a new data breach at service operator Transport for London (TfL).

The data leak affected users of TfL’s Oyster photocards – which are provided to children and students, the over-60s, military veterans and people participating in apprenticeship schemes, among other things.

It is understood to include names, email and home addresses, phone numbers, birthdates and security questions, but not photos, passwords, financial details, or data relating to journeys made on London’s transport network.

TfL technology strategy and revenue director Shashi Verma said: “The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologise to our customers affected by this incident.”

TfL has taken the photocard system offline to prevent any malicious access and reported the incident to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO). Affected users have also been contacted. It hopes to restore the service as soon as possible.

Speaking to the BBC, Verma revealed the breach came to light on Monday 16 November when photocard users received unexpected emails asking them to validate their TfL accounts, prompting an internal investigation.

In a statement, Verma said that the speed with which TfL had identified and closed down the attack meant its impact was more limited than it might otherwise have been.

He added that the compromised system had been subject to cyber security testing within the past 12 months, and pointed to the extensive work done in this regard following the 2024 Scattered Spider attack on its systems – for which two men were jailed earlier this year.

At the same time, he acknowledged that new hacking tools and techniques keep bubbling up, more so now than ever. “This is a very difficult game to keep up with,” he said.

Muhammad Yahya Patel, virtual chief information security officer (vCISO) and cyber security advisor for EMEA at Huntress, said: “265,000 people woke up to find their personal details in someone else’s hands through no fault of their own.

title: Ukrainian police arrest former members of Conti ransomware group
raw_text:
Ukrainian police have arrested four cyber criminals as part of an investigation conducted in cooperation with the FBI, claiming they are part of a much wider ransomware gang responsible for $40m of extorted funds from victims.

“The organisation comprises at least 27 people from different countries, including Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Russia. The associated broader criminal structure has more than 60 participants in eight jurisdictions. Among them are former members of the famous group of Conti hackers,” said a statement from the Ukrainian national police.

“At least 28 companies have transferred more than $40.5m in ransom to hackers,” they added. “The attackers stole 1.4 terabytes of data from a US company and extended the attack to other companies in the same group. Initially, they demanded $10m. Following the negotiations, they received $5m.”

The police said that, before being launched, “each attack [had] been carefully prepared. The attackers studied the company’s financial situation, assets, employees, and information system vulnerabilities. The targets were companies in the oil and gas, pharmaceutical, industrial and logistics industries, financial institutions and critical infrastructure facilities.”

This methodology is consistent with what has been known about the practices of the Conti gang since its disappearance in early 2022, following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

“To access corporate networks, the authors posed as members of the IT support service, obtained login credentials and convinced employees to install remote access software,” the Ukrainian police said.

This practice refers to the BazarCall subgroup that specialised in establishing initial access to targeted systems for the benefit of two teams in particular within Conti - one that will have led to the Quantum ransomware, then Royal and BlackSuit, and the other leading to Black Basta, of which traces of former members have been found in other ransomware groups such as ThreeAM or Cactus.

According to Ukrainian police, cyber criminals have even “created their own platform with voice messages generated by artificial intelligence.” This suggests a BazarCall affiliation to Silent Ransom Group (SRG), whose internal leaks have recently been analysed by the Ransom-ISAC.

The infrastructure of the cyber criminal group BlackSuit was seized by law enforcement in July 2025, as part of an international operation called “Checkmate” - a valuable source of information that has potentially allowed authorities to identify other actors related to this group.

The operation was coordinated by Europol. The Ukrainian police helped confirm Quantum's affiliation to the Chaos group, passing through Royal and BlackSuit. Documents from Ukrainian court decisions provide elements confirming this assertion, openly mentioning Chaos.

Some US victims are explicitly named, starting with the Warren Oil Company, which is believed to have paid $5m in ransom in August 2024, but also Newpark Resources and Maxxis International, as well Quantum Health, which was attacked earlier this year. The Maxxis attack was claimed by the BlackSuit group in November 2024.

title: UK court confirms existence of government surveillance order against Apple
raw_text:
A British court has confirmed that the Home Office has issued a secret order to provide police and intelligence services with the capability to access encrypted data stored by users of Apple devices.

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal found that government claims that confirming the existence of the order, known as a Technical Capability Notice (TCN), would damage national security were unfounded.

The tribunal rejected arguments from the Home Office that revealing the existence of the secret order, which has been widely reported in the press, and publicly referred to by senior members of the Trump administration, would damage national security. It found that the Home Office had failed to consistently follow its policy of neither confirming nor denying (NCND) the existence of the order, undermining government arguments that it should remain secret.

The case represents the second time this year that the government has been forced to back down on assertions of NCND to protect claimed government secrets. It follows the Agent X case, in which MI5 was found to have lied to two courts and misled an oversight body to protect a neo-Nazi informant who had abused his partner.

Existence of TCN already confirmed

Three judges found today (19 November) that despite the UK government’s claimed secrecy over the order issued to Apple, government officials had confirmed the existence of the TCN to newspaper journalists and to US government officials.

A leak to the Washington Post first revealed that the Home Office issued a technical capability notice to Apple in January 2025 requiring it to provide access to end-to-end encrypted messages and data stored by Apple’s customers worldwide in iCloud.

The existence of the order was confirmed by the former US director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, in a post on X in August 2025, which exceeded three million views, after the US administration raised concerns that the order would allow the UK to access data on American citizens.

The court also found that UK government officials gave briefings to the Times and the Financial Times confirming the existence of the secret order.

Apple, Privacy International and Liberty are challenging the home secretary’s legal powers to issue technical capability notices to technology companies in the Investigatory Powers Tribunal.

Apple’s legal arguments against the Home Office

Apple is bringing five core legal arguments challenging the home secretary’s powers to issue technical capability notices (TCNS) against tech companies:

  • Does the home secretary have powers to issue warrants for targeted interception of communications outside the United Kingdom?
  • Can the home secretary’s statutory powers be used to regulate security or privacy services offered by a technology company to its customers?
  • Was the consultation process which the Home Office is required to conduct before issuing a technical capability notice lawful?
  • Does the technical capability notice amount to disproportionate interference with people’s rights under the European Convention on Human Rights?
  • Has Apple been treated differently from other technology companies (for example, similar companies have not been issued with a TCN) by having a TCN issued against it?

The government can use TCNs to require tech companies to modify their services to provide police and intelligence services access to their users’ data. Rather than comply, Apple withdrew its Advanced Data Protection (ADP) service from UK users, stating: “We have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products and services and never will.”

The tribunal found that the government had not consistently applied its policy of neither confirming nor denying the existence of the order. Two different reputable newspapers had reported that government officials departed from NCND and positively confirmed the existence of the technical capability notice, it said.

Claims by the Home Office that internal leak investigations failed to find a government source that passed the information on to the press had “little or no evidential value”.

The home secretary had the opportunity to file detailed evidence about internal investigations to a closed hearing of the tribunal but had chosen not to do so, and ministers and government officials chose not to provide statements to the court.

Briefings to media and US officials

The judges inferred that the briefings to newspapers did take place and were authorised by government ministers, senior officials or special advisers.

“It is extremely unlikely that multiple government sources would have briefed the media in the absence of authorisation for such a briefing,” the court found.

The court also found that the UK government had given Apple permission to brief US government officials about the order, without any apparent assurance of confidentiality in what “amounted to a further clear departure from NCND”.

The court noted that it was “abundantly clear” by April 2025 that most senior US officials and politicians were not prepared to keep the order secret, as they regarded it as an “egregious breach” of US citizen’s First Amendment rights.

The cumulative effect was that anyone with even a passing interest in the topic would already know that the Home Office had served a technical capability notice on Apple, the judges found. Anyone could find out the answer to whether a TCN had been issued against Apple by simply typing the question into Google’s chatbot.

The judges agreed with Apple and the NGOs that the home secretary had not established that it would be damaging to national security to confirm the existence of the technical capability notice. The decision will mean that the court will be able to hear arguments over the lawfulness of the home secretary’s powers to issue TCN’s in public hearings.

Judges will decide whether details about the technical capability notice can be disclosed without damaging national security or the public interest in future hearings.

Apple is challenging the lawfulness of the home secretary’s powers to issue TCNs under five grounds (see box). Most of the arguments can be heard in open court without damaging national security, the IPT found today.

Caroline Wilson Palow, legal director at Privacy International, said that the decision was a major victory for transparency and effective oversight, adding: “The Investigatory Powers Tribunal has rightly rejected the UK government’s attempts to shield from scrutiny an issue of immense public interest – whether Apple has been ordered to undermine the security of our devices – based on an unsupported claim of a risk to national security. The government should not be allowed to use its policy of ‘neither confirm nor deny’ as an impenetrable shield.”

Akiko Hart, director of Liberty, said that end-to-end encryption was vital to protect personal information and to securely communicate.

“Encryption protects the things that matter most to us – including our family photos, personal messages, bank details and health records. At a time of growing cyber threats, governments should be rising to the challenge to strengthen digital security protections rather than opening the door to hackers and hostile actors,” she added.  

A Home Office spokesperson confirmed the existence of the TCN, saying that the right to privacy should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public: “Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so.

“Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies,” the spokesperson added.

  • 10 February 2025: Apple: British techies to advise on ‘devastating’ UK global crypto power grab – A hitherto unknown British organisation, which even the government may have forgotten about, is about to be drawn into a global technical and financial battle, facing threats from Apple to pull out of the UK.
  • 13 February 2025: UK accused of political ‘foreign cyber attack’ on US after serving secret snooping order on Apple – US administration asked to kick UK out of 65-year-old UK-US Five Eyes intelligence sharing agreement after secret order to access encrypted data of Apple users.
  • 14 February 2025: Top cryptography experts join calls for UK to drop plans to snoop on Apple’s encrypted data – Some of the world’s leading computer science experts have signed an open letter calling for the home secretary to drop a controversial secret order to require Apple to provide access to users’ encrypted data.
  • 21 February 2025: Apple withdraws encrypted iCloud storage from UK after government demands ‘backdoor’ access – After the Home Office issued a secret order for Apple to open up a backdoor in its encrypted storage, the tech company has instead chosen to withdraw the service from the UK.
  • 26 February 2025: US intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard probes UK demand for Apple’s encrypted data – A secret order issued by the UK against Apple would be a ‘clear and egregious violation’ if it provides backdoor access to Americans’ encrypted data, says US director of national intelligence.
  • 5 March 2025: Apple IPT appeal against backdoor encryption order is test case for bigger targets – The Home Office decision to target Apple with an order requiring access to users’ encrypted data is widely seen as a ‘stalking horse’ for attacks against encrypted messaging services WhatsApp, Telegram and Signal.
  • 11 March 2025: Secret London tribunal to hear appeal in Apple vs government battle over encryption – A secret tribunal is due to meet at the High Court in London to hear tech giant Apple appeal against a Home Office order to compromise the encryption of data stored by its customers on the iCloud service worldwide.

  • 2 April 2025: Apple has appealed to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal over an order by home secretary Yvette Cooper to give the UK access to customers’ data protected by Advanced Data Protection encryption. What happens next?
  • 7 April 2025: Investigatory Powers Tribunal rejects Home Office arguments that identifying the ‘bare details’ of legal action by Apple would damage national security, leaving open the possibility of future open court hearings.
  • 15 April 2025: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal is a semi-secret judicial body that has made significant legal rulings on privacy, surveillance and the use of investigatory powers. What does it do and why is it important?
  • 5 June 2025: US politicians are calling for Congress to rewrite the US Cloud Act to prevent the UK issuing orders to require US tech companies to introduce ‘backdoors’ in end-to-end encrypted messaging and storage.
  • 11 June 2025: Government using national security as ‘smokescreen’ in Apple encryption row – Senior conservative MP David Davis says the Home Office should disclose how many secret orders it has issued against telecoms and internet companies to Parliament.
  • 11 June 2025: WhatsApp seeks to join Apple in legal challenge against Home Office encryption orders – WhatsApp today applied to intervene in an Investigatory Powers Tribunal case that is considering the UK’s ability to issue a technical capability notice on Apple to ‘weaken encryption’.
  • 12 June 2025: Apple encryption row: Does law enforcement need to use technical capability notices? History shows that law enforcement can bring successful prosecutions without the need for the Home Office to introduce ‘backdoors’ into end-to-end encryption.

  • 23 July 2025: WhatsApp is refused right to intervene in Apple legal action on encryption ‘backdoors’ – Investigatory Powers Tribunal to hear arguments in public over lawfulness of secret UK order requiring Apple to give UK law enforcement access to users’ encrypted data stored on the Apple iCloud.
  • 19 August 2025: US says UK has agreed to drop encryption ‘backdoor’ demands against Apple – US and UK end diplomatic row over UK encryption ‘backdoor’ order against Apple, but it remains unclear whether Apple will restore advanced encryption services to UK users.
