title: Lloyds Bank shares learnings from doing artificial intelligence at scale
raw_text:
Lloyds Banking Group has made public its learnings from integrating artificial intelligence (AI) at scale through a guide offering “real-world experiences”.

In Responsible AI: A practical guide for organisations, the bank, which has a 28 million-strong customer base, shares advice on making a “meaningful difference” through AI while managing risks and ethical considerations.

The bank’s head of responsible AI, Suzanne Brink, said using the technology shouldn’t be the goal in itself for organisations. “We need to focus on where it can make a meaningful difference for customers, colleagues and businesses,” she said. “We always start by asking not only whether we can use AI, but whether we should, and how we can do so responsibly.”

Brink said the bank decided to share what it has learned “because many organisations are grappling with the same questions”.

“Responsible AI isn’t about holding back innovation,” she said. “It’s about giving organisations the confidence to pursue the opportunities where AI can genuinely add value, while maintaining the trust of the people it is designed to serve.”

In the guide, the bank shares “real-life examples” of responsible AI in practice, including implementing AI to assist customers, as well as examples of guardrails.

The bank points to three key lessons: embedding responsible AI expertise from the start; testing controls and guardrails rigorously and monitoring AI after deployment; and making evidence-based decisions that balance the value AI and risks.

Read more about AI at Lloyds Bank

  • Lloyds Bank to train all staff on artificial intelligence.
  • More than 200 Lloyds Bank bosses to receive artificial intelligence training.
  • Lloyds Bank uses artificial intelligence to check trade finance documents.

According to the bank, the guide draws on the banking group’s experience introducing its AI-powered investing assistant on the Scottish Widows app, as well as the work of responsible AI specialists and product team to identify potential risks and embed responsible AI into design.

In January, the bank announced plans to train all 67,000 of its employees how to use AI this year through its AI Academy, with the aim of reaching its target of all staff being AI-literate by the end of this year.

In a June update, it said around 65,000 staff had now taken 400,000 courses through the AI Academy.

The bank is also training 200 of its senior leaders to ensure the organisation can get the most out of AI technology. The bank is working with training provider Cambridge Spark on the programme, which will embed AI skills in the leadership ranks.

Long-term strategy

In July, it said all customer interactions will be supported by AI by 2030 as the bank targets £100m in value generation. The announcement came as the bank’s CEO outlined the firm’s Accelerate 2030 Strategy.

As part of this, it aims to cut another £2bn in costs over the next four years, with AI technology a key enabler. This is on top of the same amount over the previous four years, which has contributed to a 23% increase in profits, which reached £4.2bn in the first half of 2026.

According to the bank’s own Financial institutions sentiment survey for 2025, banks are gaining huge benefits from AI, with 59% of surveyed firms reporting AI-driven productivity gains in the past 12 months, compared with 32% in the 2024 survey.

title: The fast fix for Europe’s datacentre gap may already be plugged in
raw_text:
Most of us can remember burning a finger on an old-style incandescent light bulb.

The typical bulb back then drew 60 watts of power. You might even remember that they had the wattage stamped on the bulb itself. What is truly intriguing is that those old bulbs released about 90% of their energy as heat, and only about 10% became light.

Fast forward to today and that old 60-watt light bulb's current-day LED replacement tells a different story. It produced about 800 lumens of visible light from its 60-watt rating, whereas a new LED can produce that same 800 lumens from about 9 watts. It almost stays cool enough to hold in your hand while illuminated. Same light, about one seventh of the power.

Keep that bulb in mind. It is the best picture I know of to explain what is happening in datacentres. It also shows why the gap between countries matters to people who may never see a datacentre.

Watts a household can picture

Megawatts mean little to most people, but watts in light bulbs do. So, I divided several countries' installed datacentre capacity by their populations and households, then flipped the result back into 60-watt bulbs.

These are installed IT capacity figures from national industry bodies and brokers, for 2025 or early 2026. Definitions differ a little, so read them as scale, not precision. They count capacity built, not power drawn.

An American household has nearly four bulbs of datacentre capacity behind it. A British household has one. A Spanish or Italian household has less than half of one, roughly a tenth of the American level.

Why should we care? Think of datacentre capacity the way earlier generations thought about power lines. Towns that got the lines got a head start. Studies of the 1930s US rollout found farm output held up better and property values rose where power arrived.

Capacity is the road that jobs and patients travel on.

Take the clinic. AI software helps read a scan sooner, and in England stroke software now reaches every stroke centre. An early NHS analysis linked it to treatment more than an hour sooner. Then there are the records of every patient, student and taxpayer, which sit in a building under some country's laws.

People in Madrid don't need to understand a megawatt, but they do need those services to be close, fast and affordable. Whether they get them depends on the capacity a country has built.

Waiting for Watts

Europe made hard choices about power. Germany closed its last three nuclear reactors in April 2023. Britain closed its last coal plant in September 2024. There were good reasons for both. But now datacentre builders face a long line. According to commercial property agents Colliers, UK datacentres wait more than eight years on average for a grid connection, while Ireland and Germany are also acutely grid constrained.

It would not be fully accurate to blame all the delay on power plant closures. Grid build-out, a sharp rise in demand and slow planning systems all play a part. But the effect on a community is the same. A site that waits eight years for power is eight years of services that never reach the community.

But the power is already at the door

With waits like that, the fastest solution sits in buildings that already have light bulbs lit up. In very basic terms, it means upgrading select older datacentres so the same grid connection can provision far more of its power for compute. 

Here's where the engineering matters. Older datacentres often have substantial power provisioned for cooling and other supporting systems. Upgrading that infrastructure with modern cooling equipment, variable-speed compressors and fans, and more effective power distribution can reduce the power required for those supporting systems, to allow more of the existing provisioned capacity to be allocated to compute. 

It is not the only route, since some new sites are needed and some countries lack older stock to convert. But where the queue is the bottleneck, conversion can be and often should be the quickest first step.

Reading the meter

How do we know a conversion worked? A 50MW connection doesn't tell us how much of that power is set aside for compute versus cooling and other overhead.

The datacentre metric PCE, Power Compute Effectiveness, was built for this question. PCE divides the IT compute power a site provisions by the total datacentre power it provisions. 

And PCE is a design-stage number that can be declared on a stated basis. Say a site has a PCE score of 0.6. That tells us that it sets aside 60% of its power for potential computing. The rest of the power is provisioned for cooling, conversion losses and other overhead. Say that same site scores 0.85 after conversion.

Think of the meter on your house wall. It sets a fixed supply. Heating, pumps and wiring losses take a share, and the lamps get what is left. A higher PCE doesn't mean a better bulb. It means more of the supply at the meter is set aside for the bulbs.

The picture is still loose. The LED story earlier was about efficiency; a better device making the same light from less power. PCE is about allocation. Nearly all the power a server uses ends up as heat too. PCE does not measure heat, and it does not measure real-time use. It measures how provisioned power is split. The design decides how much of the connection is set aside for the job that needs to be done.

The Open Compute Project published the PCE white paper this month. It is free for anyone to use. It is also new, but its true value depends on whether governments, utilities and operators actively adopt and use it.

When utilities and governments ration scarce connections, they should ask for a PCE figure alongside megawatts. Two projects asking for 50 MW are not the same project if one sets aside 60% for computing and the other 85%. The second provisions 12.5 MW more of the same scarce connection for compute, and that difference is what a PCE figure makes visible. A conversion still takes investment in cooling and electrical upgrades. But it starts with power that is already connected, so the wait for a connection should be shorter.

Back to the question

A burned finger taught us all that every watt goes somewhere. The meter on the wall decides how many there are to spend. Every provisioned watt is either set aside for compute or for supporting the datacentre itself. The design decides how the connection is divided.

So, what is each country's opportunity to advance, learn and establish a data-ready society? Part of the answer sits in the power it already has. The rest depends on how it divides that power.

Paul Quigley is chief strategic relations officer at Airsys Cooling Technologies and co-author of the PCE white paper published by the Open Compute Project.

summary:
Most of us can remember burning a finger on an old-style incandescent light bulb.

The typical bulb back then drew 60 watts of power. You might even remember that they had the wattage stamped on the bulb itself. What is truly intriguing is that those old bulbs released about 90% of their energy as heat, and only about 10% became light.

Fast forward to today and that old 60-watt light bulb's current-day LED replacement tells a different story. It produced about 800 lumens of visible light from its 60-watt rating, whereas a new LED can produce that same 800 lumens from about 9 watts.

title: Counting cloud carbon cost an opportunity for new businesses
raw_text:
A common claim in technology is that moving to the cloud reduces carbon emissions. Hyperscale datacentres are typically more efficient than enterprise owned infrastructure, and cloud providers have invested heavily in renewable energy and operational efficiency.

The challenge however is to prove exactly how much carbon has been avoided. For organisations that report against sustainability targets, assess cloud migration programmes or offset residual emissions, there is an awkward reality. Namely, that carbon is surprisingly difficult to measure in the public cloud. 

A business cannot meaningfully offset a number it cannot confidently measure. And in many respects cloud sustainability has become an observability problem. 

Cloud teams have detailed metrics for performance, availability and cost. But carbon is hard because the information needed to calculate it sits across operational systems, energy networks and infrastructure platforms, depends on allocation methodologies and assumptions, and often cannot be independently verified by customers.  

This is an area where there is real opportunity for high potential businesses to start, scale and reach their full potential. That’s if they can develop a frontier digital technology that offers greater insight into the carbon cost of the public cloud. As organisations place greater emphasis on understanding the environmental impact of digital infrastructure, demand is likely to grow for solutions that can translate carbon data into operational insight. 

Offsetting a number you cannot see  

The first challenge that comes with offsetting a number that a business cannot see is attribution. In a traditional datacentre, for example, an organisation owns the infrastructure and can directly measure electricity consumption. 

In the public cloud, thousands of customers share the same infrastructure. Servers, storage systems, networking equipment and cooling systems are pooled across multiple workloads, tenants and applications. The relationship between a single workload and the energy required to support it is therefore far less obvious, and hinders how businesses can assess their productivity, performance and overall costs.  

Most cloud providers offer sustainability dashboards, but these typically provide aggregated monthly estimates rather than detailed operational data. An organisation may know its cloud estate generated a certain volume of emissions during a reporting period, but not necessarily which applications or business activities were responsible. This can make it difficult for business leaders to make informed decisions on where changes can be made, and the likely outcome of such decisions that pertain to efficiency, cost and output.  

To build a more accurate picture, organisations need to combine workload data, energy data, environmental attributes such as carbon intensity, and information about the underlying infrastructure. Only by linking these different sources can they understand how digital activity translates into environmental impact. Without this level of insight, carbon accounting becomes an exercise in allocation and estimation rather than direct measurement.  

The baseline problem 

What makes it difficult to develop a solution to this problem, however, is that carbon reduction requires comparison against a baseline. Yet establishing a stable baseline in the public cloud is far from straightforward and creates a significant challenge for organisations and opportunity for high potential businesses developing frontier technologies to address it. 

Cloud environments are constantly changing. Workloads scale automatically. Applications are modernised. Data volumes increase. AI services are adopted. Infrastructure shifts between regions. The environment being measured rarely stays still long enough to make straightforward comparisons. 

Location adds another layer of complexity. Carbon intensity can vary dramatically between cloud regions and even between different times of day within the same region. 

Consider a data processing workload scheduled overnight in a region supplied primarily by wind or hydroelectric generation. Run the same workload during peak demand in a region dependent on gas fired generation and the resulting emissions may be considerably higher. Nothing has changed within the application itself. What has changed is the electricity system that supports it. 

From measurement to optimisation 

The real opportunity is not simply better carbon reporting. It is bringing operational, energy and environmental data together in a way that allows organisations to make better decisions. 

When workload data is combined with energy consumption, carbon intensity information and infrastructure characteristics, organisations gain a clearer picture of environmental impact. That creates opportunities to shift workloads to lower carbon regions, improve utilisation and make more informed operational decisions. 

More importantly, it moves sustainability beyond annual reporting and into day-to-day operations. Emerging approaches such as carbon-aware computing and carbon-aware workload scheduling move flexible workloads to locations or times where lower carbon electricity is available. This is where the challenge becomes less about accounting and more about innovation. Improving environmental performance and bringing information together could enable new tools, services and business models that help operators understand the carbon impact of digital infrastructure and its wider demands on energy systems and local resources. 

The public cloud is often more efficient than traditional enterprise infrastructure, but efficiency is not the same as transparency. Until workloads can be linked more clearly to energy use, environmental conditions and underlying hardware, organisations will continue to struggle to prove whether they are genuinely reducing emissions or simply reporting them differently. 

Frontier technologies as a foundation for change  

Addressing these challenges will require new ways of combining operational, infrastructure and environmental data. Encouragingly, high potential businesses across the UK are already beginning to tackle different aspects of the problem. 

Emerging innovators such as Greenpixie, Climatiq and Open Climate Fix demonstrate how frontier technologies that span cloud, data and AI can be applied to improve carbon transparency, support more informed decision-making and accelerate decarbonisation across the economy. From measuring the impact of cloud and AI workloads, to embedding carbon intelligence into digital systems and optimising renewable energy networks, these organisations highlight the growing opportunity for innovation at the intersection of digital technology and sustainability. 

Digital Catapult's role is to help high potential businesses bridge the gap between technological innovation and industry adoption. By working with industry partners to identify challenges, validate solutions and create routes to commercialisation, we help promising businesses demonstrate value in real-world environments and scale their impact. We do this by working across high-growth sectors including clean energy, defence, security and the creative industries.  

As organisations place greater emphasis on understanding the environmental impact of their digital infrastructure, the ability to measure, manage and optimise carbon performance is likely to become an increasingly important source of competitive advantage.

The public cloud has transformed how organisations consume computing resources. The next challenge is ensuring that environmental performance can be understood with the same level of visibility and confidence as cost, availability and security. 

Luke Sperrin is head of clean energy industries at Digital Catapult

title: US tech outages spark conversation on resilience in the age of AI
raw_text:
A series of widespread technology outages affecting a wide range of organisations across the US has sparked a discussion around business continuity and cyber resilience, and speculation over the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) systems.

From downtime affecting the likes of Apple, Microsoft and Workday, to a nationwide ground stop affecting all flights in the country after a Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) networking hardware upgrade went awry, and from interruption to consumer banking services to a confirmed network outage at the National Security Agency (NSA), the IT problems have hit home across the US.

Although the disruption has not been publicly confirmed as the result of a cyber security incident or incidents, ordinary members of the public are naturally asking the question, “Are we under attack?”.

Que sera sera

For now, the question of whether the outages are a merely unfortunate coincidence or the result of coordinated attacks on US infrastructure by a hostile power is the subject of some debate in mainstream discourse.

In response to the outages, president Trump, questioned on the situation ahead of an Asean summit in the Phillipines, was quoted as saying: “It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen.”

But this said, the wider US government has been crystal clear on its view; interviewed earlier this week, homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin said that he was virtually certain the outages were not related to a cyber attack.

Appearing before the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday 18 November, director of national intelligence Jay Clayton took a similar approach. He said: “We have no indication that these incidents are related, that they’re coordinated. We also have no indication that they’re result of a state-sponsored malign actor.”

In his interview, Mullin speculated that artificial intelligence (AI)  – which he termed super intelligence (SI) in line with directives from the president – could have played a role, and other politicians, such as Virginia senator Mark Warner, also pointed to the impact of AI.

Writing on social media platform X, Warner said that as AI made it possible to identify more issues across more systems more quickly, organisations were coming under pressure to fix them quickly and often all at once, putting strain on systems that were never designed to handle such rapid iteration.

“While we still need to get to the bottom of these incidents, the evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity,” said the senator. “Still, these disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences.”

So, are the authorities on the right track? And is AI’s impact a factor in the way that senator Warner supposes?

Steve Povolny, vice-president of AI strategy and security research at Exabeam, said it was most likely the incidents were indeed a coincidence.

“[This] sounds like a cop out, but probably isn’t,” he said. “The services on that list share a lot of plumbing underneath: the same cloud providers, DNS, certificates and networking vendors. One bad update or failed piece of equipment can take down names that look unrelated … People also notice outages in clusters and forget the quiet months.”

Povolny rejected outright the idea of a coordinated attack by nation state actors from China, Iran or Russia. “[It] would be the loudest thing a state actor has ever done, and attackers who want access usually work to keep it quiet,” he said.

Turning to the impact of AI, Povolny said there was a possibility that someone using an AI tool to move faster, or an automated change pushed live without review, could have been a factor in some of the disruption.

Security lessons in the making

While not a cyber security incident in the traditional sense of the term, there are still security lessons to be drawn from the current wave of outages, said Halcyon Ransomware Research Center vice-president Cynthia Kaiser, a former FBI operative.

“We are in an era where AI is accelerating the discovery of legacy software flaws, forcing organisations to race to patch vulnerabilities before adversaries can exploit them, which inevitably creates friction and disruptions,” she said.

“Even when an outage isn’t caused by a cyber attack, these moments of operational distraction leave dangerous gaps open for threat actors and opportunists to take advantage of, making it crucial for both institutions and everyday individuals to remain on high alert against social engineering and unsolicited outreach.”

ISC2 chief operating officer Casey Marks echoed the sentiment, saying that the so-called CIA Triad – confidentiality, integrity and availability – a foundational model for the development of security systems, already recognised that keeping critical systems accessible was as essential to effective cyber security as data protection, something that the outages have clearly highlighted.

Marks recommended that organisations take a good look at their business continuity and recovery plans.

“Start by identifying the systems your organisation can’t operate without and the vendors those systems depend on. Then test what happens when those services go down. Teams should know who can make recovery decisions, how to reach employees and customers if their usual channels are down, which operations can continue, and which systems need to come back first,” said Marks.

“A technical failure can stop a business just as effectively as an attack, even when no data is stolen. Planning for disruption and testing how you’ll recover deserve the same attention as preventing attacks,” he said.

Povolny also highlighted the similarities between a technical outage and a cyber intrusion, saying that in the throes of a crisis it can be hard to tell the two things apart.

“Services go dark, people can’t log in, and nobody yet knows whether the cause was a mistake or a break-in. The teams that sort it out fastest are the ones who already know what normal looks like for their systems and accounts. When a platform fails, they can check right away whether a privileged account did something unusual just before it,” he said.

“The teams that can’t answer that tend to either call an attack too early or wave it off too late, and both cost them. Resilience matters here too. If a company has never practiced running without its main network or cloud provider for a day, the first real outage is a poor time to learn how.”

But Vasu Jakkal, chief strategy officer at Armadin – herself a former Microsoft security leader – concluded on a more upbeat note.

“While the disruption to our day-to-day lives is a concern and there is work to be done, I’m optimistic because it means that defenders are taking the threat of AI-driven attacks extremely seriously and IT teams are working on modernising infrastructure for an agentic world,” she said.

“These organisations have recognised they need to upgrade their systems because attackers aren’t waiting until they test updates to strike. But these past few days have demonstrated that defenders are in an impossible position: either they accept the risk that hackers will exploit vulnerabilities before they’re ready to update their systems, or they rush patches faster. If given the option, they should choose the latter every single time.”

Describing the outages as growing pains, she said there was unfortunately a high likelihood of more such disruption to come. “I’m confident that we’ll move past these hiccups. It’s a process, but a necessary one to protect ourselves long-term,” said Jakkal.

title: Workday Rising EMEA: Autopiloting key to AI-led business transformation
raw_text:
At Workday’s Rising EMEA conference in Barcelona, the cloud-based HR and financial applications supplier staked out more of its artificial intelligence (AI) strategy, with an emphasis on autopiloting as a key to business transformation among its customers.

It also used the event as an opportunity to disclose its intention to acquire a company called Honeydew, described as a “semantic layer for AI and business intelligence” (BI). The prospective acquisition is said to give “AI agents and BI tools the same governed business definitions, so answers stay consistent wherever customers work”. Honeydew was founded in Tel Aviv in 2022 by former Salesforce and VMware executive Baruch Oxman.

Workday co-founder and CEO Aneel Bhusri (pictured above), who left the company in January 2024 and returned to the helm in February 2026, opened the keynote by saying his plan has been to emulate Steve Jobs when he returned to Apple in 1997 and simplified the business. The idea, Bhusri said, is to refound Workday as a quasi-startup.

The bulk of the keynote was driven by Gerrit Kazmaier, president of product and technology at Workday, with leading roles also played by chief AI officer Joel Hellermark and vice-president of AI engineering Alet Blanken. All three are relatively new to Workday. None were in place in 2024.

In the keynote, Kazmaier said AI represented an opportunity to rethink business processes and redesign workflows. “AI is not a game of quantity. The winners won’t be the ones with the most AI. The winners are going to be the ones who apply it the best. Many think of AI as an efficiency gain – fewer, flatter, lower. That all sounds really good, at first sight. But if you stop there, you’re going to miss out on the real opportunity. Real AI transformation is about driving real growth.”

In an interview with Computer Weekly, Kazmaier said: “Many in the software industry are not seeing the big picture. You could easily treat AI as a technology topic. But when we talk to our customers and other companies, that is different from what they care about. For them, it is always people and process first.”

Part of the strategy, he said, is to create AI autopilots. “They are basically an AI solution that solves a particular problem. They are not a set of technologies for self-assembly. When you look out there, a lot of AI gets delivered in the form factor of prompts and templates. Our strategy is different. It is to deliver these AI autopilots for our customers.”

In the keynote, Kazmaier said the supplier’s “work intelligence” functionality, embedded in its agentic platform, plays a role in enabling companies to transform how work gets done. This capability deconstructs jobs into their underlying tasks and skills rather than treating a “job” as a single fixed unit.

In an executive Q&A session at the conference, he said more about why Workday thinks “work intelligence” is important for how its customers want to do AI-enabled change at scale.

“All of our customers, and indeed any organisation, including Workday, is right now navigating the AI transformation. Everyone is trying to figure out how to create a hybrid workforce that consists of human and AI workers, and how they should conceptualise that,” said Kazmaier.

“When we think about AI transformation, the level of understanding required is not at the level of jobs or job descriptions. It’s actually something new, a new atom of work, which is the task,” he added.

“Work intelligence basically is an analysis, reasoning and intelligence layer that introspects all of your data that you have in Workday and then maps out a strategic workforce transformation plan for your company and precisely describes all of the steps that you need to take from automation, through human augmentation to [purely] human.”

Honeydew acquisition

The Honeydew acquisition is a new element in Workday’s AI approach. The supplier’s statement about the intended acquisition said: “AI is only as good as the definitions behind it. A dashboard, a chat experience, and an AI agent might each answer ‘what’s our headcount?’ differently based on its own definition.”

Honeydew is said to capture and map multiple definitions and pull the right definition based on the person or agent asking, the specific use case, and the situational context. 

Workday’s chief technology officer, Gabe Monroy, said: “An AI model shouldn’t be improvising the calculation behind a payroll number. With Honeydew, the model says what it needs, and Workday builds the exact query, the same way every time, within each person’s or agent’s permissions.”

Yasmeen Ahmad, senior vice-president and general manager of Workday Data Cloud, who also spoke in the keynote, said of the acquisition: “The greatest bottleneck in enterprise AI today isn’t reasoning, it’s context. Foundation models know language, but they don’t naturally understand the physics of your business. By embedding Honeydew into Workday Data Cloud, we will provide a living semantic graph to give autonomous agents the exact, governed business context they need to safely execute at the core.”

Sovereignty in Europe

At the event, the supplier also announced what it described as new governance and operational safeguards for Workday EU Sovereign Cloud. These include a dedicated EU-based company to operate Workday EU Sovereign Cloud under European leadership. The supplier will establish a company based in Ireland to operate the service, and its board will be made up of senior Workday leaders who are EU citizens.

Kazmaier said: “European organisations shouldn’t have to choose between adopting AI or sovereign controls for their sensitive HR and finance data. Workday runs the critical systems that pay people and close the books, so we’re bringing sovereign protections to the applications where that work happens, without slowing innovation.”

The service will run on the Amazon Web Services (AWS) European Sovereign Cloud, which runs as a distinct independent partition, separate from the AWS commercial cloud.

title: I am the passenger: In Brussels at Google’s data sovereignty event
raw_text:
As Mr I Pop so astutely pointed out, it’s from the viewpoint of the passenger that you see “the city’s ripped backsides”. And this is very much the case as our Eurostar creeps into Brussels.

Many main railway stations have less than salubrious surroundings, and that’s the case with Brussels Midi. As my driver nudges the Merc slowly away from the chaotic station frontage, the surroundings are down at heel, and jumbled architecturally and ethnically, as the  Express Afro-Indian warehouse sits alongside Centro Asturiano (a non-profit cultural association) and Alice Carroll – Atelier Galerie.

10 minutes further on and we strike out onto a wide boulevard. Sat in a traffic jam, I realise we’re in the embassy district. That’s a Bahraini flag overhanging the grand frontage beside me. Others soon slide past – Brazil, Saudi, Romania, Tanzania, etc.

Diplomatic baggage

I’m in Brussels for Google’s AI Sovereignty Symposium, and embassies are a good thing to consider here. They are a microcosm of what sovereignty is all about in the real world. Law enforcement in the country in which they are sited is not allowed in without express permission, and, of course, diplomatic baggage allows for movement in and out of almost any object without interference. That’s an incredibly clear set of boundaries.

Data sovereignty is a different kettle of fish. Even located in their own country, organisations do not have the level of data security from foreign law enforcement an embassy has in a foreign one. And, of course, here we’re really talking about security from US agencies, which have laws that allow them to compel US companies to provide data and to gag the company from revealing that. If we also take into account Five Eyes collaboration, then that scenario could potentially work across the countries involved there too.

The result is a lot of confused and confusing talk around data sovereignty. There are undoubtedly people that believe, and people who would lead them to believe, that simply placing data in a local cloud region somehow makes it sovereign. But it is not. Nobody who has really examined the issue of data sovereignty is under any illusion.

But back to Brussels

Twenty-five minutes or so after leaving the station, we’re on a peripheral boulevard. Wide. Leafy. Wooded out beyond the edges of the city, off to our right.

And we arrive. A bronzed-glass brutalist structure (pictured), and apparently somewhere inside is a hotel (Mix Brussels), but from the outside it looks like a municipal library or museum.

I float around the first evening reception at the Google event attempting to fend off hunger with multiple breadsticks and olives, and I chat with some people.

In the room

One chap, from a DC-based think tank, says “No serious person in this room is going to tell you that a European organisation can be in partnership with an American company and be truly sovereign with the powers of the CLOUD Act and FISA 702.”

Then there’s a lady from a neocloud company. She says her interest in data sovereignty is because her company offers sovereign datacentres. “But what about the hardware or the software if it comes from an American company?” I ask. She’s frank. “The hardware can never be sovereign,” she says.

I’m prepared to accept that such comments are typical of anyone who’s really looked into the question. So, it seems, is Google.

Google’s pitch

Next day, as the morning keynotes progress, it soon feels like Google is cheerleading European strength as an independent bloc. It’s not altogether a foolish move. Google offers air-gapped solutions, and those in which local partners can run cloud solutions based on Google technology where updates and keys can be handled outside of Google’s control. These approximate most closely to something we’d recognise as providing sovereignty. They also offer the (completely illusory) guarantees of data residency within specific regions, of course, which routinely route data / metadata to foreign parts as part of the cloud provider’s global operations.

But, it seems to me, that here Google has realised it can’t ignore a growing realisation in Europe that IT infrastructure should be far less dependent on US companies, and is building a strategy to sell itself as a partner to those companies and states that realise this.

title: How sovereign do we need to be? Data sovereignty as a spectrum
raw_text:
The US Cloud Act and FISA 702 give Washington the power to compel US companies to hand over data, wherever it sits. Meanwhile, Five Eyes intelligence sharing widens potential data snooping to US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand collaboration.

So, what sovereignty guarantees remain when such mechanisms potentially allow cloud data to be accessed by law or bilateral agreement, and when a US provider can be compelled to write or push a patch into systems anywhere in the world?

That’s the question Google executives were asked at its Sovereign AI Summit in Brussels this week, where the company argued sovereignty is a spectrum and that customers should choose their point on it.

Jai Haridas, vice-president of regulated and sovereign cloud at Google Cloud, did not dodge the legal point. “We are a US company, and we have to follow the US laws,” he said.

But he pointed to architectural responses made possible in Google white-labelling of its technology to national cloud offerings. There aren’t many deployments to point at, but one is PREMI3NS – a sovereign cloud offering built on Google Cloud Dedicated technology and operated by S3NS – which received SecNumCloud 3.2 qualification from France’s National Agency for the Security of Information Systems (ANSSI) in 2025.

Under SecNumCloud, for example, “all updates go into quarantine where they are tested by the operator Thales, and they can actually stop an update”, Haridas said.

If there’s a spectrum, such measures are near the strong end of it.

At the summit, Google announced functionality that aims to make such a spectrum realistic for customers. These included a preview of confidential external (ie, customer) key management and audit frameworks, which extend the three-tier sovereign portfolio – data boundary, dedicated cloud and distributed cloud – it launched last year.

Meanwhile, analysts at Omdia are working on a five-level maturity model to help organisations work out where they sit:

  1. At level one, sovereignty is not a focus. We find reliance on third-party infrastructure, in unregulated firms with speed and cost unrestricted by sovereignty concerns.
  2. Level two offers improved visibility, but still no control, through public cloud offers that add privacy and guaranteed local residency features.
  3. Level three describes regulated industries that are still mostly reliant on cloud provider infrastructure but may need direct control over critical data and software via sovereign cloud solutions where law and regulation compel them.
  4. Level four gives public bodies with high geopolitical sensitivity – such as in the public sector – direct control over the full stack through a local partner that operates the same code base as the cloud provider, with extra-territorial access still in place.
  5. Level five is “very strong” with full control of data, software and infrastructure via national cloud providers or air-gapped solutions, and is reserved for organisations where the fundamentals of their activity would be at stake, such as defence organisations or Swiss banks.

Panel contributors at the event (pictured above) showed how such a spectrum accords with real-world practice.

Gertjan Dewaele, vice-president of product and technology at payment product company Worldline, described its dual setup – global payment workloads on public cloud, and a sovereign European stack for clients and projects such as the digital euro.

“Sovereignty for payments is not new,” he said. Regulation already pushes in this direction, such as under Dora, the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act, where financial firms must show exit plans and fully redundant systems.

Roman Kislyi from Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation described the far end of the spectrum. His ministry runs Gemini but strips out identifying data before it leaves the country, while keeping critical systems in distributed datacentres and a data embassy located abroad.

“Will your solution save the data of your citizens? Will your solution work if your datacentres are hit by a missile? Will your solution work if there is a blackout? Those are the questions we ask ourselves every day,” Kislyi said.

For manufacturers, the trade-off is different. Hamza Charrouf, chief customer officer at Pelico, said industrial customers want to keep operational knowledge out of models they do not control, and increasingly want innovation and sovereignty together rather than have to make a choice between them.

Panel members converged on a single point – the right level of control depends on what the data is for. “Take the emotion out of the domain, understand what you need, and then develop that,” said Robert Kernahan, vice-president and head of sovereign cloud for northern and central Europe at Capgemini.

“And when you break away from this one-size-fits-all idea, you go to optionality of choice, and you build that in,” he said.

Marcus Mühling, chief executive of Secure Cloud Germany, put the same point more bluntly. “If your clients have to make extreme choices – either sovereignty or innovation – that’s broken,” he said.

But cost is a key constraint. A partner-operated dedicated cloud carries a premium of 15% to 20% above standard public cloud rates, Google’s Haridas said. He described it as “a luxury product if you don’t need it”, but not if regulation requires it.

Sovereignty is clearly moving up the stack towards artificial intelligence, although that wasn’t a major topic of many conversations at the event.

But, said Mauro Capo, digital sovereignty lead EMEA at Accenture, clients now often ask who controls the models, the enterprise knowledge they draw on, and “the decisions and the actions that those models will increasingly influence”. Sovereignty, he argued, is shifting from infrastructure to data and knowledge.

For UK IT leaders, the debate may have taken place on the continent, but the spectrum of responses exists here too. The UK Ministry of Defence runs Google’s air-gapped distributed cloud variant, for example, and UK organisations that use US hyperscalers face the same Cloud Act question but without any EU-type security certification as a response.

The practical lesson is the one the panel kept returning to: Classify the data, decide the level of control each class needs, and build exit routes in from the start.

  • Data dive: Kill switch and catch-up – can Europe close the sovereignty gap? We examine whether European providers can match hyperscalers on continuity and control.
summary:
The US Cloud Act and FISA 702 give Washington the power to compel US companies to hand over data, wherever it sits. Meanwhile, Five Eyes intelligence sharing widens potential data snooping to US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand collaboration.

So, what sovereignty guarantees remain when such mechanisms potentially allow cloud data to be accessed by law or bilateral agreement, and when a US provider can be compelled to write or push a patch into systems anywhere in the world?

That’s the question Google executives were asked at its Sovereign AI Summit in Brussels this week, where the company argued sovereignty is a spectrum and that customers should choose their point on it.

Jai Haridas, vice-president of regulated and sovereign cloud at Google Cloud, did not dodge the legal point. “We are a US company, and we have to follow the US laws,” he said.

But he pointed to architectural responses made possible in Google white-labelling of its technology to national cloud offerings. There aren’t many deployments to point at, but one is PREMI3NS – a sovereign cloud offering built on Google Cloud Dedicated technology and operated by S3NS – which received SecNumCloud 3.2 qualification from France’s National Agency for the Security of Information Systems (ANSSI) in 2025.

Under SecNumCloud, for example, “all updates go into quarantine where they are tested by the operator Thales, and they can actually stop an update”, Haridas said.

If there’s a spectrum, such measures are near the strong end of it.

At the summit, Google announced functionality that aims to make such a spectrum realistic for customers.

title: Unlawfully held images still used for police facial recognition
raw_text:
UK police are continuing to conduct tens of thousands of retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches on potentially millions of unlawfully retained custody images, the police watchdog has found.

In November 2026, the HM Chief Inspector of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS) published a 58-page report examining how police forces and the National Crime Agency (NCA) are using RFR, after being commissioned by UK home secretary Shabana Mahmood to investigate the matter a year earlier.

Unlike live facial recognition (LFR), which captures and compares people’s faces to a pre-determined watchlist in real time, RFR is applied to already-captured images retroactively, enabling police to compare “probe” images against existing custody images taken when suspects are arrested.

The Home Office originally added an a RFR function to the Police National Database (PND) in 2013, allowing trained and licensed police users to search custody images to identify unknown persons of interest.

As it stands, the PND – which collates data from all 43 police forces in England and Wales, as well as Police Scotland, the Police Service of Northern Ireland, the National Crime Agency and other law enforcement bodies – contains billions of records drawn from several hundred databases, including more than 20 million facial images.

According to the watchdog, its inspection revealed that custody images are still being retained in breach of police information management rules, which set out how forces should review, retain and dispose of custody images.

It noted that while custody image deletion was largely outside the scope of its inspection – which instead focused more on governance arrangements and operational practices – it nonetheless found that “some of the images used in RFR searches should have been deleted and yet were still available for RFR searches”.

It added that this creates a situation that “risks undermining public confidence” in how police are using the technology.

As it stands, UK law enforcement bodies are making more than 300,000 RFR search requests per year.

On top of issues around unlawful custody image retention, the watchdog also found that police use of RFR technology lacked consistent oversight and safeguards, describing a legal and regulatory landscape that is fragmented and underdeveloped.

The “limited oversight”, it added, is compounded by inconsistent approaches to public consultation, transparency and record-keeping across forces, as well as “considerable variation” in how individual forces are using the tech itself.

It also found that police forces often did not have enough management information to understand how effectively they used RFR, or to evaluate the technology’s contribution to crime investigations. This means forces generally “couldn’t clearly show performance improvements from using RFR”.

A long-standing issue

Although it is not mentioned in the report, a High Court ruling in 2012 found the retention of custody images in the PND to be unlawful, on the basis that information about unconvicted people was being treated in the same way as information about people who were ultimately convicted. It also ruled that the six-year retention period was disproportionate.

Despite the 2012 ruling, successive biometric commissioners have warned that millions of custody images are still being unlawfully retained.

Writing to other chief constables to outline some of the issues around custody image retention in February 2022, the National Police Chiefs Council (NPCC) lead for records management, Lee Freeman, said the potentially unlawful retention of millions of custody images “poses a significant risk in terms of potential litigation, police legitimacy and wider support and challenge in our use of these images for technologies such as facial recognition”.

However, HMICFRS said in its report that it was “reassured” by a project launched in October 2023 by the Home Office and NPCC – known as Programme Tabula – to manage the custody image retention issue.

Responding to Computer Weekly’s questions about the custody image issue in November 2023, the NPCC said at the time that “policing needs to ensure transparency and legitimacy in the way we control the use of this important biometric information.”

While a spokesperson confirmed that a national programme had been launched a month earlier “to ensure consistency and co-ordination across UK policing in how it retains, processes and then uses custody images, particularly in the use of facial recognition”, it did not disclose the name of the programme.

“Through the programme, we will agree and implement a robust management regime for custody images to ensure compliance to agreed policies and legislation,” it said. “It is vital to public confidence that this programme is adopted nationally to make sure we are holding data lawfully and ethically, both now and in the future.”

The spokesperson added that while the programme was yet to be publicised, it will seek to establish a management regime for custody images, alongside a review of all currently held data by police forces in the UK, which will be implemented over a two-year period.

“We welcome this work,” said HMICFRS. “It is important that the police service aligns its approach to retaining custody images with other biometric data so that it is consistent and lawful. We look forward to learning how Programme Tabula will support forces in managing custody images more consistently and improving their compliance with legal and data retention requirements.”

Limited oversight

In terms of the wider oversight issues, HMICFRS found that legislation has not kept up with the technology or its use, leading to governance gaps and inconsistent oversight practices.

“Some forces had clear guidance setting out how searches should be carried out, how results should be recorded and what corroborative enquiries were required,” it wrote. “Others lacked formal procedures, which increased the risk of inconsistent decision-making and misunderstanding of the technology’s limitations.

“We found that investigators and supervisors didn’t routinely document the consideration or use of RFR in investigation plans, enquiry logs or supervisory reviews. As a result, forces often lacked clear audit trails showing how RFR results informed decision-making and whether appropriate corroboration had taken place.

“This limits forces’ ability to assess their use of RFR, identify missed opportunities, and provide effective scrutiny and governance.”

On how this translates into practical use, HMICFRS said that police investigators did not always know that RFR results were intelligence rather than evidence, and therefore required further enquiries before officers took enforcement action.

“This creates a risk that people could be incorrectly identified or arrested, which could undermine public confidence in the technology,” it said.

“We found that some investigators didn’t always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches. In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action.”

His Majesty’s Inspector of Constabulary Kathryn Stone said continued public support relied on showing the technology was being used properly.

“Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment,” she said. “A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence.”

Upcoming legislation

In December 2025, the Home Office launched a 10-week consultation on police use of biometrics, including LFR, allowing interested parties and members of the public to share their views on how the controversial technology should be regulated. This also covered other forms of biometric surveillance, including RFR.

This followed on from then-home secretary Yvette Cooper telling a Lords committee in July 2025 that the government intended to create “a proper, clear governance framework” to regulate the use of facial recognition technology by police.

When launching the consultation, the Home Office said that although a “patchwork” legal framework for police use of facial recognition technology exists – including for increasing use of retrospective and “operator-initiated” versions – it does not give police forces the confidence to “use it at significantly greater scale … nor does it consistently give the public the confidence that it will be used responsibly”.

While the government reiterated its intention to bring forward a new legislative framework for police use of biometrics in its formal consultation response, it has so far refrained from committing to specific safeguards, outside of establishing a new independent oversight body (which will consolidate and expand the functions of existing oversight roles) and committing to making public participation in oversight of a statutory requirement.

The government said the framework “will ensure policing can innovate in a repeatable and consistent manner, supporting adoption of emerging biometric and overt surveillance technologies that improve policing effectiveness and public protection, while maintaining appropriate safeguards and oversight”.

title: Former Italian PM centre stage as Google champions EU sovereignty
raw_text:
Europe can no longer be “competitive, sovereign and small” at the same time, Enrico Letta told an audience in Brussels this week. The former Italian prime minister – and now dean of politics, economics, and global affairs at IE University in Madrid – was speaking at an event hosted by Google, rather than the European Parliament or a national capital.

“In the past, the discussion about sovereignty, dimension and competitiveness was a very simple discussion,” he said. “In the past, you were able to be competitive small, and sovereign at the same time. Today, you can’t be competitive, sovereign and small. You need to be integrated in something bigger, and this is what we need to do, to scale up.” 

Letta spoke at Google’s Sovereign AI Summit in Brussels this week, where the US hyperscaler argued that European strength and European sovereignty can advance together.

Marianne Janik, who leads Google Cloud’s operations across EMEA North, opened the event with a message that presaged Letta’s. “AI will shape the next decade of Europe’s public service, healthcare and finance, and has to happen under European control,” she said.

Janik said the same four questions surfaced “in conversation after conversation”. Namely: Who can access our data and can we prove to regulators that our controls work? How do we keep AI running reliably? Will choosing more control mean settling for less capable AI? And will the value created with AI stay in Europe?

Her answer was that Google can help organisations with all four of these. “Keep your options open at every layer,” she told delegates, describing a stack that customers can compose from European partners, open models and Google’s own infrastructure.

The company used the summit to put Gemini models into Google Cloud Dedicated, preview confidential external key management and add audit frameworks. These extend the three-tier sovereign portfolio – data boundary, dedicated cloud and distributed cloud – it launched last year. It also launched an accelerator for sovereign AI startups and said more than a dozen software suppliers, including European providers, had validated their products on its dedicated cloud.

Letta, author of the 2024 report Much more than a market, argued that Europe’s problem is fragmentation rather than a lack of ambition. He wants a “28th regime”, a European code of business law that lets firms scale across the bloc without 27 national rulebooks.

“I don’t want Europe being a protectionist fortress,” he said. “I would like to see Europe stronger, more integrated, able to recuperate 25 years of non-integration.”

He framed the debate around what he called the “cost of non-innovation”, borrowing from the 1988 Cecchini report on the cost of non-integration that underpinned the single market. The same method, he argued, should now apply to technology. Namely, every regulation that slows adoption carries a price that rarely appears on the ledger.

He was also clear that the answer is not to shut out US technology. “If you think that now we get total energy independence in one year, total financial independence in one year, total tech independence in one year, I think it’s totally unrealistic,” he said. Trust, he added, “is the most relevant value in our world”, and “mutual trust between Europe and the US is also politically fundamental”.

The politics turns on CADA, the Cloud and AI Development Act, which European institutions are still negotiating. Google’s stage guests warned that a restrictive reading would be expensive. Discussion cited an ECIPE paper that put the migration bill at €80bn across the next decade and warned of an eight-year delay to innovation.

The fault line is whether CADA should favour “made in Europe” providers or stay open to trusted non-European firms that operate through local partners. Google is lobbying hard for the latter, and its guests echoed the argument that exclusion would raise costs without improving security.

Giorgia Albetino, senior director and head of government affairs and public policy for Google Cloud EMEA, put it directly. “I don’t believe that only made-in-Europe will really serve the interests of Europeans,” she said.

The dependency argument ran through the event. Timo Kleiner, director of future networks at the European Commission, said “dependency is a problem” when a single provider fails. “Dependencies, when they are too significant, become risks,” he said, referring to the disruption caused by a global IT outage the previous week.

Marcus Mühling, chief executive of Secure Cloud Germany, put the customer view plainly: “If your clients have to make extreme choices – either sovereignty or innovation – that’s broken.”

The event was not a one-way conversation. Roy Illsley, an analyst at Omdia, read the display as a competitive move. “Google is trying to create a difference between its approach and their rivals,” he said. “They are playing the ‘open’ card, which has been under-used as a contingency or alternate supply.”

Oracle has Alloy, AWS has its European Sovereign Cloud, and Microsoft is “playing catch up”, Illsley argued. Google’s enthusiasm for European integration, on this reading, is a way to stand apart from the pack.

It might appear puzzling that a US hyperscaler would platform explicit European advocacy. But Google has a commercial interest in the outcome. A louder European voice on sovereignty helps shape CADA in a direction that keeps hyperscalers inside the tent, and it positions Google as the partner of choice for governments that want control without giving up frontier AI.

For UK IT leaders, the event matters less as a product launch than as a signal. UK CIOs should be watching how far CADA reaches, since many run workloads in EU regions and face the same questions about who can access data.

Google has brought an interesting pitch – a company subject to US law, arguing for European strategic autonomy. It has made the argument louder than its rivals and attached a product portfolio to it.
